Generative AI, Large Language Models, and Coding Agents Foundations, adaptation, evaluation, and practical Claude workflows Davut Ayan 2026-10-21 Introduction This book combines two formerly separate sets of study notes: foundations of generative AI and large language models, and practical workflows for working with Claude and AI coding agents. The goal is to connect model concepts with safe, reproducible practice for data science and software work. The book has three parts: LLM foundations — transformers and attention, pre-training and scaling laws, fine-tuning and PEFT, evaluation, alignment (RLHF, DPO), and building LLM applications (inference optimization, RAG, tools, responsible AI). Prompt engineering — prompt anatomy, techniques, use-case strategies, evaluation, and safety (in progress). Applied agent workflows — prompting, code review, verification loops, Claude Code hooks and skills, and reproducible notebooks. An appendix summarizes the hands-on labs that accompanied the LLM foundations material. These are educational notes, not vendor certification material. Product features change quickly, so product-specific chapters link to primary vendor documentation and should be checked against the installed product version. How to use this book Read the LLM chapters in sequence when learning the underlying concepts. Use the Claude chapters as practical references for agent-assisted work. Run and inspect generated code; do not treat model output as validated merely because it is fluent. Protect secrets and private data, use least-privilege tool permissions, and keep a human reviewer responsible for consequential decisions.

These chapters began as study notes from the DeepLearning.AI / AWS course Generative AI with Large Language Models (Coursera). They have since been rewritten as a reference, checked against the primary papers cited in each chapter, and extended with later developments. 1.1 What generative AI is Generative models learn the statistical structure of their training data and produce new samples from it: text, images, audio, video, or code. This book focuses on large language models (LLMs): neural networks trained on very large text corpora to predict the next token. Chatbots, code assistants, and writing tools are applications built on top of that one capability. Key terms: Foundation model. A model trained broadly enough to be adapted to many downstream tasks. Examples include BERT, GPT, T5/FLAN-T5, BLOOM, and Llama. Its capabilities must be measured on each task; they cannot be assumed from its size. Parameters. The learned weights, currently up to hundreds of billions for large models. Parameters encode distributed statistical patterns, not a database of retrievable facts. More parameters add capacity, but data, training recipe, and adaptation matter as much. Prompt, completion, inference. The text you send is the prompt. Producing text is inference. The output is the completion. Context window. The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once: instructions, conversation, documents, tool results, and its own output. The limit varies by model; check current documentation. You interact with an LLM in natural language, not in a formal programming language. You can use it as is, or adapt it (Chapter 3) without training a new model. 1.2 What LLMs are used for Many tasks reduce to next-token prediction under the right prompt: Generation: drafting essays, emails, or marketing copy. Summarization: condensing dialogues, documents, or reviews. Translation: between natural languages, or from natural language to code or SQL. Information extraction: pulling named entities (people, places, organizations), fields, or labels out of text. Augmented tasks: answering from documents or calling APIs. These are not abilities of the model alone; the surrounding application supplies the data and tools (Chapter 5). Larger models generally handle more tasks without examples. Smaller or specialized models can still be the better choice on cost, latency, privacy, or a narrow task. Choose by evaluating on your own use case. 1.3 Before transformers: recurrent networks Earlier language models used recurrent neural networks (RNNs). An RNN reads tokens one at a time and carries a hidden state forward, so in principle it summarizes everything seen so far. In practice it has three problems: Long-range dependencies. Gradients shrink (or explode) as they flow back through many time steps, so plain RNNs struggle to learn from distant context (Bengio et al. 1994). LSTMs reduced but did not remove the problem (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997). Sequential computation. Step \(t\) needs the result of step \(t-1\). Training cannot be parallelized across positions, which limits model and data scale. A fixed-size bottleneck. The whole history must be squeezed into one state vector. Language needs wide context. Words have several meanings: a bank can be a financial institution or a riverside. Sentences can be syntactically ambiguous: in “The teacher taught the students with the book”, whose book is it? Resolving such cases often requires the whole sentence or document. Attention was the fix. It was first added to RNN translation models: the decoder learned to look back at all encoder states and weight the most relevant ones (Bahdanau et al. 2015). The transformer took the next step and dropped recurrence entirely. 1.4 The transformer “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al. 2017) introduced the transformer. It is built from attention and position-wise feed-forward layers, with no recurrence. Two properties explain its success: Parallelism. All positions in a sequence are processed at once. That makes training efficient on GPUs and allows much larger models and datasets. Direct context. Every token can attend to every other token in one step, however far apart they are. 1.4.1 From text to vectors Tokenization. Text is split into tokens from a fixed vocabulary. Tokens are usually subword units learned by algorithms such as byte-pair encoding (Sennrich et al. 2016), so rare words split into pieces. Each token maps to an integer ID. A model must always be used with the tokenizer it was trained with. Embedding. Each token ID is mapped to a learned vector of dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) (512 in the original transformer). Tokens with related meanings end up close together in this space. Positional information. Attention by itself ignores order, so position must be added. The original paper added fixed sinusoidal positional encodings to the embeddings. Many modern LLMs instead use rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which encode relative position inside the attention computation (Su et al. 2024). 1.4.2 Self-attention Each token’s vector \(x_i\) is projected into three vectors with learned matrices. The query \(q_i = x_i W^Q\) says what the token is looking for. The key \(k_j = x_j W^K\) says what each token offers. The value \(v_j = x_j W^V\) is what gets passed along if the token is attended to. Stacking these vectors into matrices \(Q, K, V\) gives scaled dot-product attention: \[ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V \] \(QK^\top\) scores how relevant every token is to every other token. The softmax turns each row of scores into weights that sum to one; plotted as a grid, these weights form an attention map. Each output is a weighted average of the value vectors. Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)? Dot products grow with the vector dimension \(d_k\). Large scores push the softmax towards a one-hot output, where gradients become very small. Scaling keeps training stable. Multi-head attention runs \(h\) attention operations in parallel, each with its own projections (the original used \(h = 8\) heads of size \(d_k = 64\)), and concatenates the results. Different heads learn different relations, for example syntactic agreement, coreference, or topic. Which relation a head learns is not chosen in advance. Cost. The score matrix is \(n \times n\) for a sequence of \(n\) tokens, so attention compute and memory grow quadratically with context length. That is why long contexts are expensive. 1.4.3 The rest of a transformer block Each layer (block) wraps attention with: a position-wise feed-forward network: two linear layers with a nonlinearity, applied to each token separately (inner width 2,048 in the original); residual connections and layer normalization around both sub-layers, which make deep stacks trainable. The original model stacked six such layers in the encoder and six in the decoder. A final linear layer maps each output vector to one logit per vocabulary token, and a softmax turns the logits into a probability distribution over the next token. 1.4.4 Encoder, decoder, and the three model families The encoder reads the whole input with bidirectional self-attention. It produces a contextual representation of each input token. The decoder generates output one token at a time. Its self-attention is masked (causal): each position sees only earlier positions, so the model cannot peek at the token it is predicting. In an encoder–decoder model, the decoder also uses cross-attention, where its queries attend over the encoder’s outputs. Using one or both halves gives three families: encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT, Llama), and encoder–decoder (T5, BART). They differ in pre-training objective and in which tasks they suit. Chapter 2 compares them in detail. 1.4.5 Generating text, end to end Take translation with an encoder–decoder model, from “J’aime l’apprentissage automatique” to “I love machine learning”: Tokenize the French sentence with the model’s tokenizer. The encoder processes all input tokens in parallel into contextual representations. The decoder starts from a start-of-sequence token. Attending to its own previous outputs and (through cross-attention) to the encoder’s representations, it produces a distribution over the next token, and one token is chosen. The chosen token is appended and fed back in. Step 3 repeats until an end-of-sequence token is produced or a length limit is reached. Detokenize the output tokens into text. A decoder-only model works the same way without the encoder. The prompt and the tokens generated so far form one sequence, and the model extends it one token at a time. This loop is autoregressive generation. How the next token is chosen from the distribution is set by the generation configuration (Section 1.6). 1.4.6 Landmark models Model Year Family Size Why it matters BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) 2018 Encoder 110M (Base), 340M (Large) Bidirectional pre-training with masked language modelling; set the pattern of pre-train then fine-tune for understanding tasks T5 (Raffel et al. 2020) 2019 Encoder–decoder Up to 11B Framed every task as text-to-text; FLAN-T5 is its instruction-tuned version GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) 2020 Decoder 175B Showed strong few-shot in-context learning at scale BLOOM (BigScience Workshop 2022) 2022 Decoder 176B Open-science, multilingual (46 natural and 13 programming languages) LLaMA (Touvron et al. 2023) 2023 Decoder 7B–65B Smaller models trained on more tokens; led a wave of open-weight models Model families move quickly. Use this table for the historical milestones, and check current model cards for anything newer. 1.5 Prompting and in-context learning Prompt engineering is designing the input so the model produces the desired completion. Its most important effect, discovered at scale, is in-context learning (ICL): the model picks up a task from examples placed in the prompt, with no weight updates (Brown et al. 2020). Zero-shot: an instruction and the input, no examples. For example, “Classify this review: … Sentiment:”. One-shot: one solved example before the real input. Few-shot: several solved examples, ideally covering the label space (for example, both a positive and a negative review). What to know: ICL depends on scale. Large models often do well zero-shot. Small models may fail even with several examples. Examples cost context. They use up the context window and add tokens to every call. There is a ceiling. If a handful of examples does not get the performance you need, more examples rarely help. That is the signal to fine-tune (Chapter 3). The Prompt Engineering part of this book (starting with Chapter 6) covers prompt structure, techniques, and evaluation in depth. 1.6 Configuring generation At each step the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Inference-time settings (as opposed to training parameters) decide how the next token is picked from it, and when to stop. Max new tokens. A cap on the number of generated tokens. Generation can stop earlier at an end-of-sequence token. Greedy decoding. Always pick the most probable token. It is deterministic and fine for short factual outputs, but prone to repetitive loops in longer text. (Beam search, which keeps the best few partial sequences, is a deterministic alternative common in translation.) Random sampling. Draw the next token in proportion to its probability. This adds variety but can wander into low-probability, incoherent tokens. In Hugging Face Transformers, sampling is enabled with do_sample=True. Top-k sampling. Sample only from the \(k\) most probable tokens, renormalized. Top-p (nucleus) sampling. Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\). The candidate set adapts to how confident the model is (Holtzman et al. 2020). Temperature. Rescale the logits before the softmax: \(p_i \propto \exp(z_i / T)\). \(T < 1\) sharpens the distribution (more predictable). \(T > 1\) flattens it (more varied). \(T = 1\) leaves it unchanged. Worked example. Suppose the next-token logits are apple \(= -1.0\), banana \(= 0.5\), cake \(= 2.0\), and donut \(= 1.2\). Next token \(T = 0.5\) \(T = 1.0\) \(T = 2.0\) apple 0.002 0.029 0.094 banana 0.040 0.130 0.200 cake 0.797 0.581 0.423 donut 0.161 0.261 0.283 At \(T = 1\): Top-k with \(k = 3\) keeps cake, donut, and banana and renormalizes them to 0.598, 0.269, and 0.133. Top-p with \(p = 0.8\) keeps cake and donut, the smallest set whose cumulative probability (0.842) reaches 0.8, and renormalizes them to 0.690 and 0.310. Apple can never be sampled under either filter. In practice, use low temperature or greedy decoding for extraction, classification, and code. Use moderate temperature with top-p for open-ended writing. Hosted APIs may expose only some of these settings, and reasoning models may fix them. 1.7 The generative AI project lifecycle An LLM project moves through four stages, and later results often send you back to an earlier one: Stage Key decisions Covered in Scope Define the use case narrowly: which tasks, which inputs, what counts as success This section Select Use an existing foundation model (the usual choice) or pre-train your own Chapter 2 Adapt and align Prompting first, then fine-tuning or PEFT, then alignment with human feedback; evaluate at every step Chapters 3 and 4 Integrate Optimize for inference; add retrieval and tools to overcome model limits; deploy, monitor, and manage risks Chapter 5 Scoping matters most. A model that must do many things needs to be larger and more general than one that only extracts named entities from invoices. A narrow scope makes model choice, evaluation, and risk assessment easier and cheaper. The inner loop is adapt → evaluate → adapt. Start with prompt engineering and in-context learning. Measure against a held-out evaluation set. Fine-tune only if prompting falls short. Then return to prompting with the tuned model. Even a well-adapted model invents information when unsure and is unreliable at exact computation. It also knows nothing after its training cut-off. Production systems therefore add retrieval, tools, and verification around the model; see Chapter 5. 1.8 Key takeaways An LLM is a next-token predictor trained on huge text corpora. Many tasks, from summarization to translation to extraction, are next-token prediction under the right prompt. RNNs struggled with long-range context and could not parallelize. Transformers replaced recurrence with attention, which made large-scale training practical. Scaled dot-product attention, \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\), lets every token weight every other token. Multi-head attention learns several relations at once. The cost is quadratic in sequence length. Encoder (bidirectional), decoder (causal, autoregressive), and encoder–decoder (cross-attention) models suit different tasks. In-context learning (zero-, one-, few-shot) adapts behaviour without training but is limited by scale and context. Greedy, top-k, top-p, and temperature control the trade-off between determinism and diversity at inference. The lifecycle is scope → select → adapt and align → integrate, with evaluation throughout. 1.9 Interview checkpoints Why did transformers replace RNNs? Parallel training across positions, and direct attention between any two tokens instead of a long chain of recurrent steps. Write the attention formula. Why the \(\sqrt{d_k}\)? \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\). Without scaling, large dot products saturate the softmax and shrink the gradients. What are Q, K, and V? Learned projections of each token: what it is looking for (query), what it offers to be matched on (key), and the content it passes on when attended to (value). Why multi-head attention? Several heads can capture different relations in parallel at the same total cost. Why does attention need positional information? Attention treats its inputs as an unordered set; positional encodings or RoPE inject word order. What does causal masking do? It stops each decoder position from seeing future tokens, so training matches left-to-right generation. What is the complexity of self-attention in sequence length? Quadratic, \(O(n^2)\). Top-k vs. top-p? Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens. Top-p keeps a variable number whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\). What does temperature do? It divides the logits before the softmax. Lower values sharpen the distribution; higher values flatten it. Zero-shot vs. few-shot? When do you move to fine-tuning? Few-shot includes solved examples in the prompt. Move on when a handful of examples does not reach the target performance, or when context or cost limits bite. References

Chapter 2 Pre-training and Scaling Large Language Models After scoping a use case, the next lifecycle decision (Section 1.7) is which model to build on. Almost always the answer is an existing pre-trained model. This chapter explains why, covering: how pre-training works; why training large models strains GPU memory, and the techniques that make it feasible (number formats and distributed training); the scaling laws that link model size, data, and compute; and the narrow case where pre-training your own domain model can be worth it. 2.1 Choosing a starting model Open models are distributed through model hubs such as Hugging Face. Each model ships with a model card (Mitchell et al. 2019). The card records the intended uses, training data and procedure, evaluation results, and known limitations. Read it before anything else. It tells you whether the model’s architecture, licence, languages, and context length fit your task. 2.2 Pre-training objectives and architecture families Pre-training is self-supervised learning on a very large text corpus. The labels come from the text itself, so no human annotation is needed. What the model learns to do depends on its training objective, and the objective is tied to its architecture: Family Pre-training objective What the model sees Good at Examples Encoder-only (autoencoding) Masked language modelling: predict randomly masked tokens Both sides of each token (bidirectional) Classification, named-entity recognition, embeddings BERT (Devlin et al. 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2019) Decoder-only (autoregressive) Causal language modelling: predict the next token Only earlier tokens (left-to-right) Text generation; at scale, zero-shot and few-shot on many tasks GPT (Brown et al. 2020), BLOOM, Llama Encoder–decoder (sequence-to-sequence) Varies. T5 uses span corruption: masked spans are replaced by sentinel tokens, and the decoder reconstructs them Encoder: whole input; decoder: earlier outputs Translation, summarization, input-to-output tasks T5 (Raffel et al. 2020), BART The two main losses, for a token sequence \(x_1, \dots, x_T\): \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{causal}} = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{masked}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\setminus \mathcal{M}}) \] Here \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of masked positions. BERT masks about 15% of tokens (Devlin et al. 2019). Today’s general-purpose LLMs are almost all decoder-only. Encoder models remain the workhorses for classification and embeddings. Data. Pre-training corpora contain trillions of tokens drawn from web crawls, books, code, and curated collections. Raw web text needs heavy processing: language identification, quality filtering, deduplication, removal of personal data, and toxicity filtering. This usually discards a large share of the raw crawl. If you ever plan to pre-train, budget data collection for that loss. Filtering reduces some risks but does not guarantee unbiased or safe data. 2.3 Why training does not fit on one GPU Storing a model is cheap compared with training it. At 32-bit precision each parameter takes 4 bytes, so 1 billion parameters need 4 GB just for the weights. Training also needs, for every parameter: Component FP32 training (bytes/param) Mixed-precision training (bytes/param) Weights used in forward/backward 4 2 (16-bit copy) Gradients 4 2 Adam optimizer: momentum + variance 8 8 (kept in FP32) FP32 master copy of weights — 4 Total, before activations 16 16 Activations come on top. These are the intermediate outputs saved for the backward pass, and they grow with batch size and sequence length. Activation checkpointing saves memory by storing only some activations and recomputing the rest during the backward pass (Chen et al. 2016). Rules of thumb: Training needs roughly 4–6× the memory of the FP32 weights. That is about 16 GB for a 1B-parameter model before activations, and around 24 GB with a typical allowance for activations. A 175B-parameter model needs about 2.8 TB for weights, gradients, and optimizer states alone. No single GPU comes close. Fine-tuning has the same profile when all weights are updated. That is the main motivation for PEFT (Section 3.5). Two levers reduce the problem: smaller number formats (next section) and splitting the work across GPUs (the section after). 2.4 Number formats and quantization A floating-point number has three parts: a sign bit, exponent bits that set the range, and fraction (mantissa) bits that set the precision. Format Sign / exponent / fraction bits Bytes Largest value \(\pi\) stored as FP32 1 / 8 / 23 4 \(\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\) 3.1415927 FP16 1 / 5 / 10 2 65,504 3.140625 BF16 1 / 8 / 7 2 \(\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\) 3.140625 INT8 8-bit integer, \(-128\) to \(127\) 1 Set by a scale factor Depends on the scale (see below) FP16 vs. BF16. Both use 2 bytes and, for \(\pi\), give the same rounded value. The difference is range. FP16 overflows above 65,504, so FP16 training needs loss scaling to keep small gradients from underflowing to zero (Micikevicius et al. 2018). BF16 (brain floating point, from Google Brain) keeps FP32’s 8 exponent bits. It trades precision for the full FP32 range, which makes training more stable. That is why it became the default 16-bit training format on hardware that supports it. Mixed-precision training runs the forward and backward passes in 16-bit but keeps an FP32 master copy of the weights for the optimizer update (Micikevicius et al. 2018). This gives most of the speed and activation-memory benefit of 16-bit arithmetic while preserving update accuracy. Integer quantization maps real values to integers through a scale factor \(s\). With symmetric quantization, \(q = \text{round}(x / s)\) and \(s = \max|x| / 127\). Precision therefore depends on the range of the values being quantized. For example, if the largest weight magnitude in a tensor is 4.0, then \(s = 4/127 \approx 0.0315\). \(\pi\) is stored as \(q = 100\) and recovered as \(100 \times 0.0315 \approx 3.150\). Choosing \(s\) well is the central problem. Quantization-aware training learns the scale factors during training. Post-training quantization estimates them afterwards (Section 5.1.2). Current practice (October 2026). BF16 mixed precision is the baseline for training. Recent accelerators also support 8-bit floating-point (FP8) formats. Large models have been trained with FP8 mixed precision, for example DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI 2024). For inference, 8-bit and 4-bit weight quantization are routine. 2.5 Distributed training Multiple GPUs serve two purposes: speed (process more data in parallel) and capacity (fit a model that one GPU cannot hold). 2.5.1 Data parallelism (DDP) Distributed data parallel (PyTorch DDP) puts a full copy of the model on every GPU and gives each GPU a different slice of every batch. After the backward pass, gradients are averaged across GPUs (an all-reduce), so every copy applies the same update and stays identical. DDP speeds up training almost linearly, but each GPU must hold the full model, its gradients, and its optimizer states. It adds speed, not capacity. 2.5.2 Sharding: ZeRO and FSDP Under DDP, every GPU stores identical copies of the same states, which is pure redundancy. ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) shards these states across the \(N_d\) data-parallel GPUs instead, in three progressive stages. With \(\Psi\) parameters and mixed-precision Adam (2 + 2 + 12 bytes per parameter), the memory per GPU is: Stage What is sharded Memory per GPU 7.5B params, 64 GPUs Baseline (DDP) Nothing \(16\Psi\) 120 GB ZeRO-1 Optimizer states \(4\Psi + 12\Psi / N_d\) 31.4 GB ZeRO-2 + gradients \(2\Psi + 14\Psi / N_d\) 16.6 GB ZeRO-3 + parameters \(16\Psi / N_d\) 1.9 GB Stages 1 and 2 cut memory by up to about 4× and 8×. Stage 3 cuts it in proportion to the number of GPUs. The example column is the paper’s own illustration. Fully Sharded Data Parallel (PyTorch FSDP) (Zhao et al. 2023) implements the same idea natively in PyTorch: Before computing a layer, each GPU gathers that layer’s full parameters from the other GPUs (all-gather). It runs the forward or backward computation, then frees the gathered copy. After the backward pass, gradients are reduced and re-sharded (reduce-scatter), so each GPU updates only its own shard. The cost is extra communication. FSDP exposes this trade-off as a sharding strategy: Full sharding: most memory saved, most communication. No sharding: equivalent to DDP. Hybrid sharding: shard within a machine and replicate across machines, keeping heavy traffic on fast local links. CPU offload: parameters or optimizer states can be moved to CPU memory, at a further speed cost. 2.5.3 Model parallelism Sharding still runs each layer whole on one GPU at a time. The largest models also split the computation itself: Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. This is the Megatron-LM approach (Shoeybi et al. 2019). It needs very fast interconnects, so it is usually kept within one machine. Pipeline parallelism places different layers on different GPUs and streams micro-batches through them to keep all stages busy (Huang et al. 2019). Frontier training combines data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism (“3D parallelism”) with sharding. As GPU count grows, communication overhead lowers the throughput per GPU. That is a real cost when planning a training run. 2.6 Scaling laws Pre-training minimizes next-token loss. Three quantities determine how low the loss goes: model size \(N\) (parameters), dataset size \(D\) (training tokens), and compute \(C\). For dense transformers, training compute is approximately \[ C \approx 6ND \quad \text{FLOPs.} \] Large budgets are often quoted in petaFLOP/s-days. One petaFLOP/s-day is \(10^{15}\) operations per second sustained for a day, which is \(8.64 \times 10^{19}\) FLOPs. GPT-3 175B, trained on 300B tokens, used about \(3.14 \times 10^{23}\) FLOPs, or roughly 3,640 petaFLOP/s-days (Brown et al. 2020). That matches \(6 \times 175\text{B} \times 300\text{B}\). 2.6.1 Kaplan et al.: loss follows power laws Kaplan et al. (2020) found that test loss falls as a power law in each of \(N\), \(D\), and \(C\), provided the other two are not the bottleneck. For example, \(L(N) \approx (N_c / N)^{\alpha_N}\) with \(\alpha_N \approx 0.076\). On log–log axes these are straight lines over many orders of magnitude. That makes loss predictable: small, cheap runs forecast the loss of large ones. In practice compute is the hard constraint (hardware, time, money). The practical question is therefore: for a fixed compute budget, how should it be split between a bigger model and more data? Kaplan et al. recommended putting most extra compute into model size. That reasoning shaped the very large models of 2020–21. 2.6.2 Chinchilla: scale data and parameters together Hoffmann et al. (2022) revisited the question with more careful experiments, including learning-rate schedules matched to each run’s length. They fitted the loss as \[ L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}. \] Here \(E\) is the irreducible loss of the data, and the two other terms are the penalties for finite model size and finite data. Minimizing this subject to \(C \approx 6ND\) gives the main result: \(N\) and \(D\) should grow in roughly equal proportion, which works out to about 20 training tokens per parameter. This is a historical empirical estimate for their model family and setup, not a universal constant. The test: Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) used the same compute as Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens). It outperformed Gopher, GPT-3, and other much larger models on a wide range of downstream tasks. Measured against the 20× rule, many earlier models were over-parameterized and under-trained: Model Parameters Chinchilla-optimal tokens (~20×) Actual training tokens GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) 175B ~3.5T 300B BLOOM 176B ~3.5T ~366B Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) 70B ~1.4T 1.4T LLaMA-65B 65B ~1.3T 1.4T Interpreting scaling laws: They predict pre-training loss, not specific downstream abilities. Individual skills can improve unevenly. They hold for the architecture, data mixture, and recipe they were fitted on. Change those and you must re-fit. “Compute-optimal” optimizes training compute only. It ignores the cost of serving the model afterwards. Current practice (October 2026). The last point changed practice. A model that will serve billions of requests is cheaper overall if it is smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter (Sardana et al. 2024). Llama 3’s 8B model, for example, was trained on about 15T tokens, close to 1,900 tokens per parameter (Llama Team, AI @ Meta 2024). “Over-training” small models is now normal. Chinchilla remains the reference point for the training-compute trade-off. 2.7 Domain adaptation and pre-training your own model You rarely need to pre-train. The exception is a domain whose language is poorly represented in general corpora: Rare terms: legal terms such as mens rea and res judicata. Everyday words with special meanings: consideration in contract law means the value exchanged that makes an agreement binding, not kindness. Shorthand: a prescription note like “1 tab po qid pc & hs” means one tablet by mouth four times a day, after meals and at bedtime. A model learns its vocabulary and representations in pre-training. Later stages build on those, so a domain the model barely saw may be handled poorly. Before committing to from-scratch training, climb this ladder of options, from cheapest to most expensive: Prompting and retrieval (Chapter 5). Fine-tuning or PEFT on domain tasks (Chapter 3). Continued (domain-adaptive) pre-training. Keep pre-training an existing model on unlabelled domain text. Gururangan et al. (2020) showed consistent downstream gains from this across biomedical, computer-science, news, and review domains. Pre-training from scratch on a mixed domain and general corpus. 2.7.1 Case study: BloombergGPT BloombergGPT (Wu et al. 2023) is the best-known from-scratch domain model: Model and data. A 50.6B-parameter decoder trained on a corpus of about 51% financial text (Bloomberg’s own and public financial data) and 49% general public text. The general data preserved broad language ability. Compute. About 1.3 million A100 GPU-hours. Scaling choices. The authors used Chinchilla scaling laws to size the model for their budget, and the parameter count landed close to compute-optimal. The training tokens (569B) fell short of the compute-optimal amount, because there was not enough high-quality financial text. Real data limits forced a trade-off. Result. The paper reports that BloombergGPT outperformed similarly sized open models on financial tasks by clear margins while staying competitive on general-purpose benchmarks. The lesson is that from-scratch domain pre-training is justified only when the domain language is distinctive, high-quality domain data exists at scale, and the compute budget is large. Current practice (October 2026). Given how capable general models now are, combined with continued pre-training, fine-tuning, and retrieval, from-scratch domain pre-training is a rare choice. Justify it with an evaluation showing that the cheaper options fall short. 2.8 Key takeaways Encoder-only models (masked LM) suit understanding tasks; decoder-only models (causal LM) suit generation; encoder–decoder models suit input-to-output tasks. Start from an existing model and read its model card. Training memory is about 16 bytes per parameter before activations, which is about 4× the FP32 weights. Large models therefore cannot train on one GPU. BF16 keeps FP32’s range at half the memory. Mixed precision keeps an FP32 master copy for stable updates. Integer quantization depends on a scale factor. DDP replicates the model for speed. ZeRO/FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients, and parameters for capacity, at a communication cost. Tensor and pipeline parallelism split the computation itself. Loss scales as a power law in parameters, data, and compute. Chinchilla showed that compute-optimal training scales \(N\) and \(D\) together (~20 tokens/parameter). Inference costs now push towards smaller, over-trained models. Domain pre-training (BloombergGPT) is the expensive end of a ladder that starts with prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and continued pre-training. 2.9 Interview checkpoints Masked vs. causal language modelling? Masked LM predicts hidden tokens using both sides of the context. Causal LM predicts the next token using only earlier ones. How much GPU memory does training a 7B-parameter model need? With mixed precision and Adam, about 16 bytes × 7B ≈ 112 GB before activations. That calls for sharding, or PEFT for fine-tuning. Why BF16 over FP16? The same 8-bit exponent as FP32 gives the full range, so there is less overflow or underflow and no need for loss scaling. The cost is lower precision. DDP vs. FSDP? DDP replicates everything and adds speed only. FSDP shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, which adds capacity at a communication cost. The three ZeRO stages? Shard optimizer states; then also gradients; then also parameters. What is \(C \approx 6ND\)? The approximate training FLOPs for a dense transformer with \(N\) parameters trained on \(D\) tokens. The Chinchilla result in one line? For a fixed training-compute budget, scale parameters and tokens together, at about 20 tokens per parameter. Many earlier models were under-trained. Why train beyond Chinchilla-optimal? Serving costs dominate over a model’s life. A smaller model trained on more data is cheaper to run at the same quality. When would you pre-train a domain model? When the domain language is distinctive, domain data is plentiful, the budget is large, and prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, and continued pre-training have been shown to fall short. References

Chapter 3 Fine-Tuning and Evaluation There are three ways to make a pre-trained model better at your task. Each one changes something different: Lever What changes Covered in Prompting and in-context learning Only the input; the weights stay fixed Section 1.5 and the Prompt Engineering part Fine-tuning The weights, using labelled examples This chapter Alignment with human feedback The weights, using preference signals Next chapter This chapter covers supervised fine-tuning: full instruction fine-tuning first, then parameter-efficient methods. It ends with how to measure whether the adapted model actually improved. 3.1 Why fine-tune instead of prompting In-context learning puts worked examples in the prompt (Section 1.5). It needs no training, so it should be tried first. It has four limits: Small models may not pick up the task, even from several examples. Examples use up the context window, leaving less room for the actual input, retrieved documents, or tool results. Examples are paid for on every call, in tokens and in latency. Prompts are not great at fixing a style or format across thousands of calls. Training on examples usually makes the output more consistent. Fine-tuning moves the task knowledge from the prompt into the weights. A practical rule of thumb: fine-tuning is good at teaching behaviour (a task, format, style, or domain vocabulary). It is a poor way to add facts that change. Fresh or private facts are better supplied at inference time through retrieval, which a later chapter covers. 3.2 Instruction fine-tuning Instruction fine-tuning (also called supervised fine-tuning, SFT) continues training a pre-trained model on pairs. Each pair is a prompt containing an instruction plus the desired completion: Prompt: Classify this review: "I loved this book, could not put it down." Completion: Sentiment: positive It differs from pre-training in two ways. Pre-training is self-supervised on unlabelled text. Instruction fine-tuning is supervised on labelled pairs, and the dataset is many orders of magnitude smaller. When every weight is updated, the procedure is called full fine-tuning. Its output is a new copy of the model, often called an instruct model. 3.2.1 Building the dataset Most existing NLP datasets (reviews, Q&A pairs, dialogues) are not written as instructions. Prompt template libraries such as PromptSource (Bach et al. 2022) solve this. A template wraps each record in an instruction. For example, an Amazon review can become a rating-prediction prompt, a review-generation prompt, or a summarization prompt. Using several phrasings of the same instruction (“Summarize the dialogue”, “What was this conversation about?”, …) helps the model generalize beyond one wording. The original FLAN work wrote ten templates per dataset for this reason (Wei, Bosma, et al. 2022). Split the data into training, validation, and test sets, as in any supervised problem. The test set must stay untouched until the final evaluation. 3.2.2 Training objective The model is trained with the same next-token cross-entropy loss used in pre-training, applied to the completion. For a prompt \(x\) and target completion \(y = (y_1, \dots, y_T)\): \[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta\left(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}\right) \] The loss is commonly computed only on the completion tokens. The prompt tokens are masked out, so the model is not trained to reproduce the instruction. Gradients from batches of examples update the weights over one or more epochs. The validation loss or metric is tracked to choose when to stop. Full fine-tuning has the same memory profile as training. Weights, gradients, and optimizer states must all fit in memory (Section 2.3). That cost motivates the parameter-efficient methods in Section 3.5. 3.3 Single-task fine-tuning and catastrophic forgetting If an application needs only one task, such as summarizing support chats, you can fine-tune on that task alone. Single-task fine-tuning often works with hundreds to a few thousand high-quality examples. That is tiny compared with pre-training corpora. LIMA, for example, reported strong instruction following after tuning on 1,000 curated examples (Zhou et al. 2023). Treat any number as a starting point to validate, not a requirement. Label quality and representativeness matter more than volume. The risk is catastrophic forgetting: updating the weights for one task can degrade abilities learned earlier (McCloskey and Cohen 1989). For example, a model tuned only for sentiment classification may stop doing named-entity recognition correctly, or may answer every prompt with a sentiment label. Ways to handle it, roughly in order of cost: Check whether it matters. If the deployed model only ever performs the tuned task, losing other skills may be acceptable. Mix in general data. Add a sample of general instruction data (or the earlier tasks) to the fine-tuning set. This is sometimes called replay. Regularize the update. Penalize movement of weights that mattered for earlier tasks, for example with elastic weight consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017). Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Freeze the original weights and train a small add-on (Section 3.5). Fine-tune on many tasks at once (next section). Whatever you choose, evaluate both the target task and a fixed set of capabilities you need to keep. Without the second set, forgetting goes unnoticed. 3.4 Multi-task instruction fine-tuning and FLAN Multi-task instruction fine-tuning trains on a mixture of tasks (summarization, classification, translation, question answering, code, …) at the same time. Because no single task dominates, the model improves across many tasks instead of trading them off. The cost is data: you need diverse, high-quality examples for every task in the mixture. The FLAN models are the reference example (FLAN stands for Fine-tuned LAnguage Net): Wei, Bosma, et al. (2022) fine-tuned a 137B-parameter model on more than 60 datasets phrased as instructions. Its zero-shot performance improved on task types that were held out of training. This was the key evidence that instruction tuning teaches the general skill of following instructions, not just the training tasks. Chung et al. (2022) scaled the approach to 1,836 tasks (drawn from 473 datasets in 146 task categories) and released Flan-T5 and Flan-PaLM. Two findings matter: performance kept improving as both the number of tasks and the model size grew, and including chain-of-thought examples in the mixture preserved the models’ step-by-step reasoning ability. One dataset in the FLAN mixture is SAMSum: about 16,000 messenger-style dialogues with summaries, written by linguists (Gliwa et al. 2019). It explains both the strength and the limit of a general instruct model. Flan-T5 can summarize casual chats between friends. However, a customer-support dialogue has a different structure (a customer request, staff actions, a resolution). A general model may miss key actions or invent details there. The fix is a further round of fine-tuning on data close to the deployment setting. DialogSum is a public example: about 13,000 dialogues from real-life scenarios such as hotel check-ins and service desks, each with a summary (Chen et al. 2021). In production, permissioned internal data (your own support transcripts and the summaries your team wants) is usually the better choice. Even then, evaluate hallucination, privacy, and distribution shift separately. 3.5 Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) Full fine-tuning has three practical costs: Training memory. Gradients and optimizer states are needed for every parameter. With Adam, that is several times the memory of the weights themselves. Storage. Each task produces a complete copy of the model. Forgetting. Every weight can move, which risks catastrophic forgetting. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods freeze most or all of the pre-trained weights and train a small number of parameters. That reduces the gradient and optimizer memory. The task-specific artefact can be a few megabytes instead of a full model. The frozen base also makes forgetting less likely. Note what PEFT does not remove: the frozen weights must still sit in memory for the forward and backward passes. QLoRA (below) attacks that remaining cost. 3.5.1 Three families of methods Lialin et al. (2023) group PEFT methods into three families: Family Idea Examples Selective Train only a chosen subset of the existing parameters BitFit trains only the bias terms (Ben Zaken et al. 2022); training only the top layers Reparameterization Learn the weight update in a compact, low-rank form LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) Additive Keep the original weights frozen and add new trainable parameters Adapter layers inserted inside each block (Houlsby et al. 2019); soft prompts (Lester et al. 2021; Li and Liang 2021) Selective methods are simple. They are less common for large generative models because their quality and memory savings vary a lot. The two methods most used in practice are LoRA and soft prompts. Both are explained below. 3.5.2 LoRA: low-rank adaptation Idea. Full fine-tuning learns an update \(\Delta W\) for each weight matrix \(W_0\). Hu et al. (2022) hypothesized that this update has low intrinsic rank. If so, it can be written as the product of two thin matrices. LoRA freezes \(W_0\) and trains only those two matrices: \[ h = W_0 x + \Delta W x = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\; r \ll \min(d, k) \] \(r\) is the rank, the main hyperparameter. \(\alpha\) is a scaling constant. \(A\) starts random and \(B\) starts at zero. At step 0, \(\Delta W = 0\), so training begins exactly at the pre-trained model. Only \(A\) and \(B\) get gradients and optimizer states. Parameter count. A \(d \times k\) matrix has \(dk\) parameters. Its LoRA update has \(r(d + k)\). Matrix Full update \(dk\) LoRA, \(r = 8\): \(r(d+k)\) Share trained One attention head projection in the original Transformer, \(512 \times 64\) (Vaswani et al. 2017) 32,768 4,608 14% A \(4096 \times 4096\) projection, typical of a 7B-parameter model 16,777,216 65,536 0.39% The savings grow with the matrix size. On GPT-3 175B, Hu et al. (2022) reported about 10,000× fewer trainable parameters and about 3× lower GPU memory than full fine-tuning. Quality was on par with or better than full fine-tuning on the tasks they evaluated. Inference. After training, the update can be merged into the base weights, \(W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA\). The merged model has exactly the original shape, so it adds no inference latency. Alternatively, keep the adapters separate and load a different \((A, B)\) pair per task on one shared base model. That is how one deployment can serve many tasks. Which matrices to adapt. The LoRA paper adapted the attention projections (mainly the query and value matrices). It found that adapting more matrix types at a small rank beat adapting one type at a larger rank (Hu et al. 2022). Despite a common claim, attention does not hold most of a transformer’s parameters. With the usual feed-forward width of \(4d\), the feed-forward layers hold about two-thirds of each block’s weights. The QLoRA authors found that applying LoRA to all linear layers was needed to match full fine-tuning (Dettmers et al. 2023). Choosing the rank. In Hu et al. (2022), very small ranks (even single digits) were competitive on the tasks studied. Raising the rank did not reliably help. Values from 4 to 64 are common in practice. Treat \(r\) (and \(\alpha\)) as hyperparameters to tune on the validation set. A larger rank means more capacity and more memory, not automatically better results. 3.5.3 QLoRA: LoRA on a quantized base LoRA shrinks the trainable part, but the frozen base model still has to fit in memory. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA adapters in 16-bit on top of it (Dettmers et al. 2023). Three techniques make this work: 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a 4-bit data type designed for weights that are roughly normally distributed. Double quantization, which also quantizes the quantization constants to save more memory. Paged optimizers, which move optimizer state to CPU memory during memory spikes. The paper fine-tuned a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU while preserving the task performance of 16-bit fine-tuning. Section 2.4 explains the data types involved. 3.5.4 Prompt tuning with soft prompts Prompt tuning is not prompt engineering. Prompt engineering edits the words of a prompt by hand. Prompt tuning learns a short sequence of continuous vectors, a soft prompt, that is prepended to the input embeddings (Lester et al. 2021): Ordinary (“hard”) tokens map to fixed rows of the embedding table. A soft prompt is \(p\) virtual tokens: free vectors \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times d}\) in the same embedding space, not tied to any word. The model is completely frozen. Backpropagation updates only \(P\), using the same supervised loss as fine-tuning. The trainable count is tiny. Twenty virtual tokens with \(d = 4096\) is 81,920 parameters. One soft prompt per task can be stored and swapped at inference, and a single batch can even mix tasks. Evidence. On SuperGLUE, prompt tuning trailed full fine-tuning for small T5 models. The gap closed as model size grew, and at about 11B parameters it matched full fine-tuning. It also outperformed GPT-3’s few-shot prompting by a large margin. In the same experiments, about 20 virtual tokens captured most of the gain; longer prompts added little (Lester et al. 2021). Interpretability. The learned vectors do not correspond to vocabulary tokens. Their nearest vocabulary neighbours tend to form semantically related clusters, often connected to the task. Even so, a soft prompt cannot be read like a sentence. Related method. Prefix tuning learns trainable vectors at every layer, not only at the input, giving it more capacity per virtual token (Li and Liang 2021). 3.5.5 Choosing an adaptation method Method Trainable parameters Training memory Inference overhead Typical use Prompting / in-context learning None None Longer prompts First attempt; fast iteration Full fine-tuning All Highest None Large shift in behaviour, enough data and compute LoRA Well under 1% for large models (depends on rank and layers) Low (base still in memory) None if merged Default PEFT choice; many tasks on one base QLoRA Same as LoRA Lowest (4-bit base) None if merged; quantized base otherwise Large models on limited GPUs Prompt tuning Tiny (\(p \times d\)) Low A few extra input positions Very large frozen models; many tasks Current practice (October 2026). LoRA and QLoRA remain the standard PEFT methods in common open-source tooling, such as the Hugging Face peft library. Many hosted model APIs offer fine-tuning without exposing the method. Supervised fine-tuning is now usually one stage in a pipeline that also includes preference-based alignment (next chapter). 3.6 Evaluating fine-tuned models Classifier accuracy is easy to compute because there is one right label. Generated text is harder to score. Two sentences can mean the same thing with almost no shared words (“Mike really loves drinking tea” vs. “Mike adores sipping tea”). Two others can differ by one word and mean the opposite (“Mike does drink coffee” vs. “Mike does not drink coffee”). Automatic metrics approximate quality through overlap with a human reference. That makes them cheap and repeatable, but blind to meaning. Terminology: a unigram is one word, a bigram is two consecutive words, and an n-gram is \(n\) consecutive words. 3.6.1 ROUGE ROUGE (Lin 2004) scores summaries by their overlap with reference summaries. For n-gram matches between a candidate and a reference: \[ \text{Recall} = \frac{\text{matched n-grams}}{\text{n-grams in reference}}, \qquad \text{Precision} = \frac{\text{matched n-grams}}{\text{n-grams in candidate}}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R} \] ROUGE-1 uses unigrams, ROUGE-2 uses bigrams (which are slightly sensitive to word order). ROUGE-L uses the length of the longest common subsequence (LCS) as the match count. A subsequence keeps word order but does not have to be contiguous. Mixing this up with the longest contiguous match is a common error. Worked example. Reference: “It is cold outside” (4 words). Candidate: “It is very cold outside” (5 words). Metric Matches Recall Precision F1 ROUGE-1 it, is, cold, outside = 4 4/4 = 1.00 4/5 = 0.80 0.89 ROUGE-2 “it is”, “cold outside” = 2 2/3 = 0.67 2/4 = 0.50 0.57 ROUGE-L LCS “it is cold outside” = 4 4/4 = 1.00 4/5 = 0.80 0.89 Failure modes: Meaning reversal. “It is not cold outside” gets exactly the same ROUGE-1 scores as the candidate above. Overlap does not check meaning. Repetition. “cold cold cold cold” has a ROUGE-1 precision of 4/4 = 1.00 if every repeat counts. Clipping caps each n-gram’s matches at its count in the reference. The idea comes from BLEU’s modified precision (Papineni et al. 2002). With clipping, precision becomes 1/4 = 0.25. Reordering. “outside cold it is” still scores 1.00 on clipped ROUGE-1. Order-sensitive variants catch it: ROUGE-2 F1 = 1/3 = 0.33 (only “it is” matches) and ROUGE-L F1 = 0.50 (LCS = 2). ROUGE scores are comparable only within the same task, dataset, reference set, and implementation settings (tokenization, stemming). Use them to track progress on summarization while you iterate, never as the final verdict. 3.6.2 BLEU BLEU (Papineni et al. 2002) was designed for machine translation. It is precision-oriented and combines several n-gram sizes: \[ \text{BLEU} = \text{BP} \cdot \exp\left(\sum_{n=1}^{N} w_n \log p_n\right), \qquad \text{BP} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } c > r \\ e^{\,1 - r/c} & \text{if } c \le r \end{cases} \] \(p_n\) is the clipped n-gram precision. Usually \(N = 4\) with equal weights \(w_n = 1/4\), so the exponential term is the geometric mean of the four precisions (not a simple average). The brevity penalty BP penalizes candidates shorter than the reference (\(c\) = candidate length, \(r\) = reference length). Without it, a very short output with only safe words would score high precision. BLEU was defined at the corpus level. Sentence-level BLEU is noisy and needs smoothing, because a single missing 4-gram makes the geometric mean zero. 3.6.3 Beyond overlap metrics ROUGE and BLEU are cheap diagnostics. They cannot judge factual correctness, faithfulness to the source, safety, or usefulness. A defensible evaluation combines: a representative held-out set drawn from the deployment setting; task-appropriate automatic metrics (overlap, exact match, schema validity, executable tests); structured human review with a written rubric where judgment is needed; error analysis by category and subgroup; retained-capability checks to detect catastrophic forgetting; and latency and cost. LLM-as-a-judge (using a strong model to grade outputs against a rubric) scales human-like judgments cheaply. Zheng et al. (2023) found that strong judges agree with human preferences about as often as humans agree with each other. They also documented systematic biases: position bias, a preference for longer answers, and a tendency to favour the judge’s own outputs. Calibrate a judge against human labels before trusting it. 3.7 Benchmarks Benchmarks are fixed, public task suites used to compare models across many skills: Benchmark Year What it measures GLUE (Wang, Singh, et al. 2019) 2018 Nine sentence- and sentence-pair understanding tasks (sentiment, entailment, paraphrase, …) SuperGLUE (Wang, Pruksachatkun, et al. 2019) 2019 Eight harder tasks (multi-sentence reasoning, reading comprehension, coreference), created as models saturated GLUE MMLU (Hendrycks et al. 2021) 2020 Multiple-choice knowledge and problem-solving across 57 subjects (elementary mathematics, US history, law, computer science, …) BIG-bench (Srivastava et al. 2023) 2022 204 community-contributed tasks (linguistics, common sense, mathematics, social bias, software, …); a smaller “Lite” subset keeps evaluation cost manageable HELM (Liang et al. 2023) 2022 A framework scoring models on seven metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) across 16 core scenarios, so trade-offs are visible rather than hidden in one number How to read benchmark results: Saturation. Top systems surpassed the SuperGLUE human-baseline estimate within about two years. A model matching humans on a benchmark is not human level at the general skill. This “arms race” is why benchmarks keep being replaced. Contamination. If test items appeared in the pre-training data, scores overstate ability. Prefer held-out or recently created items. Fit. A leaderboard rank says little about your task. A small evaluation set drawn from your own data is usually more informative. Holistic view. Accuracy alone hides calibration, robustness, and safety trade-offs, which is the point HELM was built to make. Current practice (October 2026). GLUE and SuperGLUE are of historical interest for frontier models, and MMLU is close to saturated. Harder successors such as MMLU-Pro (Wang et al. 2024) and the expert-written GPQA (Rein et al. 2023) took their place, along with agentic and coding benchmarks and arena-style human-preference rankings. Leaderboards change quickly; check current sources before quoting a score. 3.8 Key takeaways Try prompting first. Fine-tune when examples are not enough, the context window is tight, or the output must be consistent. Supply changing facts through retrieval, not training. Instruction fine-tuning is supervised next-token training on prompt–completion pairs. Template diversity helps generalization. Full fine-tuning on one task risks catastrophic forgetting. Always measure the capabilities you need to keep. Multi-task instruction tuning (FLAN) teaches general instruction following, shown by gains on held-out task types. PEFT trains a small number of parameters. LoRA learns a low-rank update that can be merged with no inference cost. QLoRA adds a 4-bit base. Prompt tuning learns input vectors and becomes competitive with full fine-tuning at large scale. ROUGE and BLEU measure surface overlap. They are useful for iteration and misleading as final evidence. Pair them with held-out data, human or calibrated judge review, and error analysis. 3.9 Interview checkpoints Fine-tuning vs. RAG? Fine-tuning changes behaviour, format, and style. Retrieval supplies current or private facts at inference. They are often combined. Why does LoRA add no inference latency? The update \(BA\) can be merged into \(W_0\), so the deployed model has the original shape. LoRA parameter count for a \(d \times k\) matrix? \(r(d + k)\) instead of \(dk\). Why is \(B\) initialized to zero? So that \(\Delta W = 0\) and training starts exactly at the pre-trained model. What does QLoRA add? A 4-bit NF4 frozen base, double quantization, and paged optimizers, so large models fit on one GPU. Prompt tuning vs. prompt engineering? Learned continuous vectors vs. hand-written discrete text. Prompt tuning needs training data and gradients. What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you detect it? Loss of earlier skills after fine-tuning. Detect it with a fixed retained-capability evaluation set. ROUGE-L vs. ROUGE-2? ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence (order-preserving, not contiguous). ROUGE-2 counts matching bigrams. Why does BLEU need a brevity penalty? Precision alone rewards very short outputs. Why distrust a high benchmark score? Saturation, contamination, and mismatch with the deployment task. References

Chapter 4 Aligning LLMs with Human Feedback Instruction fine-tuning (Chapter 3) teaches a model what tasks look like. It does not teach the model which of many plausible answers people actually prefer. A model trained to imitate internet text and demonstration data can still be unhelpful (it misreads the request), dishonest (it states falsehoods confidently), or harmful (it gives dangerous instructions or toxic language). Those behaviours exist in its training data. Alignment is the further training that moves a model towards human preferences. A common shorthand for the target is HHH: helpful, honest, and harmless (Askell et al. 2021). This chapter explains the classic method, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and the methods that simplified or replaced parts of it. 4.1 Why preferences instead of demonstrations Supervised fine-tuning needs a correct completion for every prompt. For many qualities (tone, helpfulness, safety, a good summary) writing the ideal answer is hard. Recognising the better of two answers is much easier. Preference data is therefore cheaper to collect and often more informative. The evidence that this works: Christiano et al. (2017) trained RL agents from human comparisons of behaviour clips, with no hand-written reward function. Stiennon et al. (2020) applied the idea to summarization. Policies trained with human feedback produced summaries that people preferred over those of much larger supervised models, and even over the human reference summaries in the dataset. Ouyang et al. (2022) (InstructGPT) used the same recipe for general instruction following. Labelers preferred outputs of the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model to those of the 175B-parameter GPT-3. This was the template for the first wave of chat assistants. 4.2 Reinforcement learning, mapped to language models In reinforcement learning, an agent follows a policy to choose actions in an environment. It observes the resulting states and receives rewards. It learns a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward. For an LLM the mapping is: RL concept In RLHF Policy \(\pi_\theta\) The LLM being trained State \(s_t\) The prompt plus the tokens generated so far Action \(a_t\) The next token; the action space is the vocabulary Episode / rollout One full completion of a prompt Reward A score for the finished completion from a reward model, usually given once at the end Humans cannot score millions of rollouts during training. RLHF therefore first trains a reward model to imitate human judgments, then optimizes the policy against that model. 4.3 The RLHF pipeline The InstructGPT recipe (Ouyang et al. 2022) has three stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Start from an instruction-tuned model, so that sampled completions are already reasonable. Reward modelling. Collect human comparisons of completions and train a model that scores a (prompt, completion) pair. RL optimization. Optimize the SFT model against the reward model with PPO, while penalizing drift from the SFT model. 4.3.1 Collecting human feedback For each prompt in a prompt dataset, the SFT model generates several completions. Labelers rank them against a defined criterion, such as helpfulness, correctness, or harmlessness. The labeling instructions matter as much as the labelers. Good instructions state the criterion, say how to fact-check, define how to treat ties (allowed but rare), and provide a flag for nonsensical answers so they can be removed. Each item usually goes to several labelers, which shows agreement and exposes labelers who misread the task. For scale: InstructGPT used about 40 contractors and ranked between 4 and 9 completions per prompt (Ouyang et al. 2022). Ranking produces pairs. A ranking of \(K\) completions yields \(\binom{K}{2}\) pairwise comparisons; three completions give three pairs. Each pair becomes a training example (prompt, preferred \(y_w\), rejected \(y_l\)). Ranking yields more training signal per prompt than a thumbs-up/down label. 4.3.2 Training the reward model The reward model \(r_\phi(x, y)\) is usually a language model (often initialized from the SFT model) with a head that outputs one scalar. It is trained with the Bradley–Terry model of pairwise preference (Bradley and Terry 1952). Under that model, the probability that \(y_w\) beats \(y_l\) is \(\sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\). The loss is the negative log-likelihood of the human choices: \[ \mathcal{L}(\phi) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\,y_w,\,y_l)} \Big[\log \sigma\big(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\big)\Big] \] Only reward differences are identified, so the absolute scale is arbitrary. Rewards are often normalized before RL. A classifier can also act as the reward. For a narrow goal such as detoxification, an existing classifier (for example, a hate-speech detector) can supply the reward. A common choice is its logit or probability for the desired class (“not hate”). This skips preference collection, but the policy is then optimized towards whatever that classifier happens to measure. 4.3.3 The RL objective and the KL penalty The policy is trained to earn high reward without drifting far from the SFT model, which is kept frozen as the reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\): \[ \max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D},\, y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)} \big[r_\phi(x, y)\big] \;-\; \beta\, D_{\text{KL}}\!\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x) \,\big\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big) \] In practice the KL term is estimated from the sampled tokens. Each generated token is charged \(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}\), and the reward-model score is added at the final token. The penalty does two things: It limits reward hacking. The reward model is accurate only near the kind of text it was trained on, so the policy should not wander into unfamiliar text. It preserves fluency and general ability learned in pre-training and SFT. \(\beta\) sets the trade-off. Too small and the policy exploits the reward model; too large and it barely moves. 4.3.4 PPO in the LLM setting Proximal Policy Optimization (Schulman et al. 2017) is the RL algorithm used in the original RLHF work. Each PPO iteration has two phases: Phase 1: rollouts. Sample completions for a batch of prompts from the current policy. Score them (reward model minus KL penalty), and record the token log-probabilities under the policy that generated them. Call that policy \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\). Phase 2: updates. Take a few gradient steps on that batch, using three terms: Value loss. A value function \(V_\psi(s_t)\) predicts the future reward from a partial completion. It is usually a separate head or model, often initialized from the reward model. It is trained by regression, \(\big(V_\psi(s_t) - \hat{R}_t\big)^2\), towards the observed return \(\hat{R}_t\). Clipped policy loss. The advantage \(\hat{A}_t\) measures how much better token \(a_t\) turned out than the value function expected. Generalized advantage estimation combines the one-step errors \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\) into \(\hat{A}_t = \sum_{l \ge 0} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}\) (Schulman et al. 2016). With the probability ratio \(\rho_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) / \pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(a_t \mid s_t)\): \[ L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\Big[\min\big(\rho_t \hat{A}_t,\; \text{clip}(\rho_t,\, 1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon)\, \hat{A}_t\big)\Big] \] Maximizing \(\rho_t \hat{A}_t\) raises the probability of tokens with positive advantage and lowers it for tokens with negative advantage. The advantage estimates are reliable only while the new policy stays close to the one that generated the data. The clip (typically \(\epsilon \approx 0.2\)) and the \(\min\) remove any incentive to move the ratio outside \([1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]\). That gives an approximate trust region, which is the “proximal” in PPO. Entropy bonus. Adding the policy’s entropy \(S[\pi_\theta]\) discourages the policy from collapsing to one fixed answer. It acts during training, whereas temperature acts at inference. The combined objective, maximized by gradient ascent, is \(L^{\text{CLIP}} - c_1 L^{\text{VF}} + c_2 S\). Here \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are weighting hyperparameters. After the updates, the new policy becomes \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\) for the next round of rollouts. Two “old” models. \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\) in the ratio is the previous iteration’s policy, and it changes every iteration. \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) in the KL penalty is the frozen SFT model and never changes. Confusing the two is a common mistake. Cost. PPO-based RLHF keeps four models in play: the policy, the reference policy, the reward model, and the value model. It is also sensitive to hyperparameters. One way to cut memory is to train the policy as a LoRA adapter (Section 3.5). The reference policy is then the same base weights with the adapter switched off, so there is no second full copy. 4.4 Reward hacking Reward hacking happens when the policy finds outputs that score highly under the reward model but fail the real objective. It is Goodhart’s law applied to a learned proxy. Typical symptoms: A detoxification run learns to fill every answer with effusive phrases (“most awesome, most incredible”) because the toxicity classifier rewards them. Answers get longer or more hedged because the reward model learned that length correlates with preference. The text degrades into odd or ungrammatical strings that happen to score well. Leo Gao et al. (2023) measured this systematically. As optimization pushes the policy further from its starting point, the proxy reward keeps rising. The true quality (measured by a larger “gold” reward model) rises, peaks, and then declines. Defences: the KL penalty against the reference policy; early stopping on held-out human or gold-model evaluation, not on proxy reward; larger and better reward models, refreshed with new comparisons from the current policy; and reading samples. Hacked outputs are often obvious to a person long before the metrics show anything. 4.5 Evaluating an aligned model Evaluate the aligned model with the same measure on the same held-out prompts, before and after. In the detoxification example, run the SFT model and the aligned model over the same evaluation prompts. Score each completion with a toxicity classifier, then compare the mean probability of the toxic class. It should go down. Also check for collateral damage: Capability regressions (“alignment tax”). InstructGPT showed drops on some standard NLP benchmarks. It reduced them by mixing pre-training gradients into the PPO updates (Ouyang et al. 2022). Over-refusal, where the model declines harmless requests. Sycophancy. RLHF-trained assistants tend to agree with the user’s stated views even when the user is wrong, partly because human raters reward agreement (Sharma et al. 2024). Human preference evaluation on held-out prompts remains the reference standard. 4.6 Scaling feedback: Constitutional AI and RLAIF Human labeling is slow and expensive, and labelers must read harmful content. There is also a tension between helpfulness and harmlessness, documented by Bai, Jones, et al. (2022). A model optimized mainly for helpfulness may comply with a harmful request, such as explaining how to break into a neighbour’s Wi-Fi. Constitutional AI (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022) replaces most of the human harmlessness labels with feedback from the model itself, guided by a short written list of principles called the constitution. An example principle: choose the response that is least likely to encourage illegal or unethical activity. It has two phases: Supervised phase (critique and revise). Prompt a helpful model with red-team prompts designed to elicit harmful answers. Ask it to critique its own answer against a principle, then to rewrite the answer to remove the problem. Fine-tune on the (red-team prompt, revised answer) pairs. RL phase (RLAIF). Sample pairs of responses from the fine-tuned model. Ask a model which response better satisfies the constitution. Train a preference model on these AI-generated comparisons (combined with human helpfulness labels in the paper), then run RL as in RLHF. This is reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF). The principles are explicit and editable, so the target behaviour is easier to inspect and adapt to a domain than thousands of individual labels. The quality of the result still depends on the principles and on the model’s ability to apply them. 4.7 Beyond PPO: current alignment methods Current practice (October 2026). PPO-based RLHF is the conceptual foundation, but it is no longer the only or default recipe. Two simpler or more targeted families are widely used. Check recent technical reports before treating any one pipeline as standard. 4.7.1 Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Rafailov et al. (2023) showed that the KL-regularized objective above has a closed-form optimal policy, \(\pi^*(y \mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp\big(r(x, y)/\beta\big)\). Inverting this expresses the reward through the policy itself. Substituting into the Bradley–Terry loss gives a classification loss on preference pairs, with no reward model and no sampling during training: \[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\,y_w,\,y_l)} \left[\log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} \right)\right] \] DPO raises the likelihood of preferred answers relative to rejected ones, measured against the reference model. It needs only the policy and a frozen reference, trains like supervised fine-tuning, and has few hyperparameters. The trade-off: it learns from a fixed, offline preference dataset, not from fresh samples of the current policy. Online RL methods can keep collecting feedback as the policy changes. 4.7.2 RL with verifiable rewards and GRPO For tasks with checkable answers (mathematics, code that must pass tests, strict formats), the reward can be a program instead of a learned model. The reward is “1 if the final answer is correct or the tests pass, else 0”. This is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Lambert et al. 2024). A rule-based reward is much harder to hack than a learned reward model. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al. 2024) is a PPO variant built for this setting. For each prompt it samples a group of \(G\) completions and uses each completion’s reward relative to the group as its advantage: \[ \hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G)} \] This removes the value model. GRPO keeps PPO’s clipped ratio and adds a KL term to the reference policy. DeepSeek-R1 showed that large-scale RL with rule-based rewards can teach a model long, self-checking chains of thought (DeepSeek-AI 2025). RLVR-style training is now a common ingredient of reasoning models. 4.7.3 Method comparison Method Feedback source Reward model? Models in memory during training Main strength Main risk RLHF with PPO Human rankings Yes, learned Policy, reference, reward, value Online; general preferences Cost, instability, reward hacking Constitutional AI / RLAIF Model judgments guided by principles Yes, learned from AI labels As PPO Scales feedback; explicit principles Inherits the judge’s blind spots DPO Human or AI preference pairs No (implicit) Policy, reference Simple, stable, cheap Offline; limited to its dataset RLVR with GRPO Programmatic checks No (rule-based) Policy, reference Hard to hack; drives reasoning gains Only for verifiable tasks 4.8 Key takeaways Alignment trains for preferred behaviour (helpful, honest, harmless), not just task format. Comparing outputs is easier for people than writing ideal ones. RLHF has three stages: SFT, a reward model trained on pairwise comparisons with the Bradley–Terry loss, and RL against that reward with a KL penalty to the frozen SFT model. PPO limits each update with a clipped probability ratio. A value function supplies advantages, and an entropy bonus keeps outputs diverse. Reward hacking is the central failure mode. Defend with the KL penalty, held-out evaluation, better reward models, and reading samples. Constitutional AI and RLAIF replace much human labeling with model feedback guided by explicit principles. DPO removes the reward model and RL loop for preference data. RLVR with GRPO uses programmatic rewards for verifiable tasks and underlies today’s reasoning models. 4.9 Interview checkpoints Why train a reward model instead of using humans directly? RL needs rewards for a huge number of samples. The reward model is a cheap, always-available stand-in for human judgment. Reward-model loss? Bradley–Terry: \(-\log \sigma\big(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l)\big)\). Only reward differences are learned. What does the KL penalty do? It keeps the policy close to the SFT model, where the reward model is trustworthy. That limits reward hacking and preserves fluency. What does PPO’s clipping do? It caps how far one update can move the probability ratio, giving an approximate trust region and stable training. \(\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}\) vs. \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? The previous iteration’s policy (in the PPO ratio) vs. the frozen SFT model (in the KL penalty). Which models does PPO-based RLHF need? The policy, reference, reward model, and value model. What is reward hacking, and how do you detect it? The proxy reward rises while true quality falls. Detect it with held-out human or gold-model evaluation and by reading samples. DPO vs. PPO? DPO is an offline classification loss on preference pairs with no reward model or sampling. PPO is online RL against a learned reward. What does GRPO remove? The value model. Advantages come from rewards relative to a group of samples for the same prompt. What is the alignment tax? Capability lost on other tasks after alignment. Mixing in pre-training data during RL reduces it. References
