Chapter 5 From Model to Application The earlier chapters cover how to choose, adapt, and align a model. This chapter covers what happens after that: making the model cheap and fast enough to serve, and connecting it to data and tools so that it can do useful work reliably. It closes with the risks specific to generative applications. Three questions shape this stage of the project lifecycle (Section 1.7): Serving constraints. How fast must completions be, what compute budget is available, and how much quality can be traded for speed or cost? External resources. Does the model need data it was not trained on, or actions in other systems? Consumption. Who calls the model (people through a UI, or other systems through an API), and what must be logged, checked, or secured on the way? 5.1 Optimizing models for inference Inference cost scales with model size. Smaller or lower-precision models load faster, need less GPU memory, and generate tokens with lower latency. The challenge is to shrink the model without losing the quality that matters for the task. Three techniques work on the model itself. 5.1.1 Knowledge distillation Distillation trains a small student model to imitate a large, frozen teacher (Hinton et al. 2015). The teacher’s full output distribution carries more information than a single correct label. It shows which wrong answers are nearly right. A temperature \(T > 1\) in the softmax, \(p_i = \exp(z_i / T) / \sum_j \exp(z_j / T)\), flattens both distributions so that this information is visible (Section 1.6 explains temperature). The student minimizes a weighted sum of two losses: \[ \mathcal{L} = \alpha \, T^2 \, D_{\text{KL}}\!\big(p^{\,T}_{\text{teacher}} \,\big\|\, p^{\,T}_{\text{student}}\big) + (1 - \alpha)\, \text{CE}\big(y,\; p^{\,T=1}_{\text{student}}\big) \] The first term (the distillation loss) matches the teacher’s softened distribution, the soft labels. The \(T^2\) factor keeps its gradient scale comparable as \(T\) changes. The second term (the student loss) is ordinary cross-entropy against the ground-truth hard labels at \(T = 1\). Distillation does not shrink the teacher. It produces a separate, smaller model that replaces the teacher at inference. DistilBERT is the classic encoder example: about 40% smaller and 60% faster than BERT, while keeping about 97% of its language-understanding performance (Sanh et al. 2019). Distillation is also standard for generative models. Two forms are common: Token-level, as above, matching the teacher’s next-token distribution. Gemma 2’s smaller models were trained this way (Gemma Team 2024). Sequence-level, where the student is fine-tuned on complete outputs generated by the teacher (Kim and Rush 2016). The small DeepSeek-R1 models were made by fine-tuning open models on reasoning traces generated by DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025). A practical pattern follows: launch with a large, capable model, collect real traffic and approved outputs, then distill or fine-tune a smaller model for that specific workload. 5.1.2 Post-training quantization Quantization stores numbers in fewer bits (Section 2.4). Quantization-aware training simulates low precision during training. Post-training quantization (PTQ) converts a model that has already been trained, so it is the usual route at deployment: Weights only or weights and activations. Quantizing activations as well saves more compute but usually costs more accuracy. Large LLMs have rare activation outliers with very large magnitude, which break naive 8-bit schemes. LLM.int8() handles them by keeping those dimensions in 16-bit (Dettmers et al. 2022). Calibration. PTQ runs a small sample of data through the model to estimate the range of values to be quantized. Error-aware methods. GPTQ quantizes weights to 3–4 bits layer by layer. It adjusts the remaining weights to compensate for each rounding error, which keeps accuracy close to the 16-bit model (Frantar et al. 2023). The result is a smaller memory footprint and often faster inference, usually with a small, measurable drop in quality. Measure that drop on your own evaluation set before deploying. 5.1.3 Pruning Pruning removes weights that contribute little. The simplest criterion is weights near zero (magnitude pruning). Methods differ in when they prune (during training, during fine-tuning, or after training) and in what they remove: Unstructured pruning zeroes individual weights. SparseGPT pruned 175B-parameter models to 50% sparsity in one shot with little loss in quality (Frantar and Alistarh 2023). Wanda reached similar results with a simpler score: weight magnitude times the norm of its input activation (Sun et al. 2024). Structured pruning removes whole neurons, attention heads, or layers. Zeros only save memory and time if the storage format and hardware can exploit them. Unstructured sparsity often gives little real speed-up. Structured or hardware-supported patterns (such as 2:4 sparsity on recent NVIDIA GPUs) are needed for actual gains. 5.1.4 Serving-side optimizations These leave the weights unchanged and optimize how tokens are generated: KV caching stores the attention keys and values of earlier tokens, so each new token is not recomputed from scratch. Memory for the cache, not compute, often limits how many requests fit on a GPU. Batching and paged KV memory. Serving systems such as vLLM manage the cache in pages to pack many concurrent requests efficiently (Kwon et al. 2023). Speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes several tokens, and the large model verifies them in one pass. The output distribution is unchanged, and latency drops when the draft is usually right (Leviathan et al. 2023). 5.1.5 Effort across the lifecycle Stage Typical effort Needs training? Main expertise Pre-training Weeks to months, very large compute Yes Architecture, data, distributed training Prompt engineering Hours to days No Task knowledge, evaluation Fine-tuning / PEFT Hours to days once the data exist Yes Data preparation, evaluation Alignment (RLHF, DPO) Fast if a reward model or preference data exist; slow if human feedback must be collected Yes Labeling design, RL or preference tuning Optimization for deployment Hours to days Sometimes (distillation) Quality-versus-cost trade-off Most applications start from an existing model and spend their effort on the bottom four rows. 5.2 Problems that training alone does not solve Even a well-adapted model has structural limits: Knowledge cut-off. The weights reflect the training data at a point in time. A model trained before a change of government will name the old prime minister with full confidence. Arithmetic and exact computation. The model predicts likely tokens; it does not calculate. Long multiplication or a tax calculation can come out close but wrong. Hallucination. Models produce fluent, specific text even when the content is unsupported. Examples include invented citations, products, or facts (Ji et al. 2023). No access to private or real-time systems. The model cannot see your order database or call your shipping API unless the application connects them. The fix is to augment the model at inference time. An orchestration layer (application code or a framework) passes user input to the model, calls external data sources and tools based on the model’s output, and returns results to the model and the user. 5.3 Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) Retrieval-augmented generation gives the model relevant external text at inference time. It does not try to store that knowledge in the weights. Retraining for every update would be slow and expensive. Retrieval keeps knowledge current, supports private data, and lets answers cite their sources. 5.3.1 The original formulation Lewis et al. (2020) paired a retriever with a generator. The retriever was a dense passage retriever (DPR) (Karpukhin et al. 2020). A query encoder embeds the question, and the closest passages are found in a pre-built index of Wikipedia passage embeddings. The generator (BART) conditions on the question plus the retrieved passages. The query encoder and generator were fine-tuned jointly, with the document index held fixed. RAG improved results on open-domain question answering over models that relied on their parameters alone. 5.3.2 A typical RAG pipeline today Most applications use the same idea without joint training: off-the-shelf embedding models, a vector index, and a general LLM. Indexing (offline): Load and clean the sources: documents, wikis, tickets, web pages. Chunk them into passages small enough to retrieve precisely, often a few hundred tokens with some overlap. Keep metadata such as source, date, and access rights. Embed each chunk into a vector with an embedding model. Store vectors and metadata in a vector store. A vector database adds keys, filtering, and updates, so each chunk can be traced back to its source document. Answering (online): Embed the query with the same embedding model. Retrieve the top-\(k\) most similar chunks, usually by cosine similarity, \(\cos(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert \lVert \mathbf{d} \rVert}\). Augment the prompt with those chunks, clearly delimited, along with an instruction to answer only from them and to cite them. Generate the answer, with citations back to the chunk sources. Retrieval is not limited to vectors. The “retriever” can be a keyword search engine, a SQL query against a database, or a web search API. 5.3.3 What makes RAG work or fail Retrieval quality caps answer quality. If the right chunk is not retrieved, the model cannot use it. Evaluate retrieval separately, for example with recall@\(k\) on labelled question–passage pairs. Chunking is a design decision. Chunks that are too large dilute relevance. Chunks that are too small lose context. Hybrid search and reranking usually help. Combine keyword search (exact names, codes, IDs) with dense search (paraphrases), then re-score the candidates with a more accurate cross-encoder or LLM reranker. Position matters in long contexts. Models use information at the beginning and end of a long context more reliably than information in the middle (Liu et al. 2024). Retrieving fewer, better chunks beats stuffing the context. Grounding reduces but does not remove hallucination. The model can still ignore, misread, or over-generalize from retrieved text. Evaluate faithfulness (is every claim supported by the cited chunks?) separately from retrieval. Access control. Retrieval must respect the user’s permissions. Otherwise RAG becomes a data-leak channel. Current practice (October 2026). Context windows are now far larger than the few thousand tokens of 2022–23 models. Check current model documentation. Long context reduces the need for aggressive chunking but does not replace retrieval. Cost, latency, position effects, and access control still favour sending only relevant material. Chapter 17 treats context selection as an engineering discipline. 5.4 Helping models reason 5.4.1 Chain-of-thought prompting Multi-step problems are a classic weakness of models that answer in one step. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting (Wei, Wang, et al. 2022) includes worked intermediate steps in the few-shot examples. The model then produces its own steps before the answer. The paper’s standard example: Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of tennis balls. Each can has 3 tennis balls. How many tennis balls does he have now? A: Roger started with 5 balls. 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is 6 tennis balls. 5 + 6 = 11. The answer is 11. Q: The cafeteria had 23 apples. If they used 20 to make lunch and bought 6 more, how many apples do they have? A: With a bare answer in the example (“The answer is 11.”), the model in the paper answered 27. With the worked steps, it reasoned 23 − 20 = 3, 3 + 6 = 9 and answered correctly. What the evidence says: CoT gains appeared mainly in large models (about 100B parameters in the original experiments). Smaller models produced fluent but illogical chains (Wei, Wang, et al. 2022). Zero-shot CoT: just adding “Let’s think step by step” also helps (Kojima et al. 2022). Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer. This improves accuracy over a single chain (Wang et al. 2023). The written chain is not guaranteed to be the real reason. Models can produce plausible explanations that hide the actual influence on their answer (Turpin et al. 2023). Treat CoT as a performance technique, not as a faithful explanation. Current practice (October 2026). Reasoning models are trained with RL to produce long internal chains of thought before answering (Chapter 4). With these models, hand-written CoT examples matter less. Reasoning effort is often a setting (a “thinking” budget) instead. The Prompt Engineering part covers prompting for reasoning in detail. 5.4.2 Program-aided language models (PAL) CoT fixes the plan but not the arithmetic: a correct chain can still contain a wrong multiplication. PAL (Luyu Gao et al. 2023) has the model write its reasoning as a program. Each reasoning step is a code comment, followed by the code that computes it: # Roger started with 5 tennis balls. tennis_balls = 5 # 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is bought_balls = 2 * 3 # tennis balls. The answer is answer = tennis_balls + bought_balls The orchestrator runs the generated code in an interpreter and returns the result. The model decides what to compute; the interpreter guarantees the computation. PAL outperformed CoT on several mathematical and symbolic reasoning benchmarks in the original paper. Today the same idea is offered as a built-in code-execution tool by model providers. Run generated code only in a sandbox. 5.4.3 ReAct: reasoning plus acting Many applications need several steps that involve external systems: look up an order, check a policy, request a shipping label, confirm an email address. ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) interleaves three kinds of output in a loop: Thought: reasoning about what to do next. Action: a call to one of a fixed set of allowed actions. In the paper’s Wikipedia question-answering tasks these were search[entity], lookup[keyword], and finish[answer]. Observation: the result of the action, which the orchestrator appends to the context before the next thought. The loop repeats until the model chooses finish. Few-shot examples teach the format, and an instruction block defines the allowed actions. Restricting the action space is essential: a model will otherwise “plan” steps the application cannot execute. In the paper, ReAct beat acting-only prompting throughout. On fact verification (FEVER) it also beat chain-of-thought. On multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA), the best results came from combining ReAct with chain-of-thought and self-consistency. The largest gains were on interactive decision-making tasks (ALFWorld, WebShop). For an LLM to drive actions reliably, its output must: name a valid action from the allowed set; be machine-parseable (a fixed syntax, JSON, a SQL statement, a script); and include the information needed to validate the action, such as the customer’s email address before a return label is sent. Current practice (October 2026). ReAct’s text-parsing loop has largely been replaced by native tool calling. The application declares tools with JSON schemas, the model emits structured tool calls, and the application executes them and returns results. The Model Context Protocol standardizes how tools and data sources connect to models (Chapter 16). Orchestration frameworks (LangChain was the early example, offering prompt templates, memory, tools, chains, and agents) are joined by vendor agent SDKs. The Thought → Action → Observation loop remains the core mental model for agents. Chapter 20 extends it to multi-agent systems. 5.5 The application stack A production LLM application has several layers, and the model is only one of them: Layer Contents Infrastructure Compute, storage, and networking, on-premises or cloud; sized for real-time or batch inference Models Foundation models and adapted models (fine-tuned, LoRA adapters, distilled students) Data and retrieval Document stores, vector indexes, databases, and their access controls Orchestration and tools Prompt templates, tool definitions, agent loops, code execution, external APIs Output handling and feedback Validation of outputs, logging, conversation memory, user feedback for later evaluation and fine-tuning Interface and security UI or REST API, authentication, rate limits, guardrails Logged prompts, completions, and feedback are a valuable asset. They become the evaluation sets and training data for the next iteration, provided users have consented and private data is handled correctly. 5.6 Responsible generative AI Generative models add specific risks to the usual ML concerns: Risk What goes wrong Mitigations Toxicity and bias Harmful, offensive, or discriminatory output, including about protected groups Curate training and fine-tuning data; alignment (Chapter 4); guardrail classifiers on inputs and outputs; diverse annotators and red-teaming Hallucination Confident, false content: invented facts, sources, or numbers Grounding with RAG and citations; tools for exact computation; faithfulness evaluation; user education and disclaimers; restrict use to suitable tasks Intellectual property and privacy Reproducing copyrighted or personal data from training or retrieval sources Data governance and licensing; filtering and blocking of protected content; policy and legal controls; machine “unlearning” is an active research area, not a solved tool Prompt injection Instructions hidden in retrieved documents, web pages, or tool outputs hijack the model, for example to leak data or trigger actions (Greshake et al. 2023) Treat retrieved and tool content as untrusted data; least-privilege tools; human confirmation for consequential actions; output validation A workable process for each application: Define the use case narrowly. The narrower the task, the easier the risks are to assess and test. Assess the risks for that use case: who is affected, and what a failure costs. Evaluate on representative data, including adversarial and subgroup cases, against explicit acceptance criteria. Monitor and iterate across the whole lifecycle. Models, data, and misuse patterns change after launch. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2023) and its generative-AI profile (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2024) are widely used, vendor-neutral references for organizing this work. Regulatory obligations (for example the EU AI Act) depend on jurisdiction and use case; check current requirements for a real deployment. 5.7 Key takeaways Distillation trains a smaller student on a teacher’s soft outputs or generated text. PTQ lowers precision after training. Pruning removes low-value weights and only speeds things up with structured or hardware-supported sparsity. Measure the quality cost of each. Serving efficiency also comes from KV caching, batching, and speculative decoding, which leave the weights unchanged. Training cannot fix knowledge cut-offs, exact computation, or access to private systems. Augment the model at inference instead. RAG retrieves relevant, permitted text and grounds the answer in it. Evaluate retrieval and faithfulness separately. RAG reduces hallucination but does not eliminate it. CoT improves multi-step reasoning in large models but is not a faithful explanation. PAL moves computation to an interpreter. ReAct’s Thought → Action → Observation loop over a fixed action set is the basis of modern tool-calling agents. The model is one layer of the application. Responsible deployment means narrow use cases, explicit risk assessment, evaluation, monitoring, and defences against prompt injection. 5.8 Interview checkpoints Why use a temperature above 1 in distillation? It softens the teacher’s distribution so that the relative probabilities of wrong answers (the “dark knowledge”) carry training signal. PTQ vs. QAT? PTQ converts a trained model and needs calibration data. QAT simulates quantization during training and usually loses less accuracy, at extra training cost. Why might pruning not speed up inference? Unstructured zeros need sparse formats and kernel or hardware support to save time. RAG vs. fine-tuning for company knowledge? RAG for facts that change or must be cited and permission-filtered. Fine-tuning for behaviour, format, and style. They are often combined. Main RAG failure points? Missed retrieval, poor chunking, lost-in-the- middle effects, unfaithful generation, and permission leaks. What is cosine similarity, and why use it for embeddings? The normalized dot product. It compares direction (meaning) independently of vector length. CoT vs. PAL? CoT writes reasoning in text and computes in the model. PAL writes code and computes in an interpreter. What are the three parts of a ReAct step? Thought, Action (from a fixed set), Observation. What is indirect prompt injection? Malicious instructions placed in content the model reads (documents, web pages, tool outputs) rather than typed by the user. References

Chapter 7 Claude Fundamentals and Product Context 7.1 Claude is a model family, not one fixed interface Claude is a family of language models developed by Anthropic. The capabilities available in a session depend on both the selected model and the product that hosts it. Claude.ai, Claude Code, an API integration, and a third-party product can expose different tools, permissions, context, and data-retention policies. Claude can work with text, code, and images. When a host provides tools, it may also search the web, read and edit files, execute commands or code, and connect to external systems. Do not infer available capabilities from the model name alone; inspect the current product, tool list, and permission settings. Primary references: Claude documentation Claude Code overview Claude tool-use overview 7.2 A practical mental model For most tasks, treat the system as four layers: Model — generates and interprets language, code, and structured content. Context — the instructions, conversation, files, and tool results visible during the current request. Tools — capabilities supplied by the host, such as file editing, Bash, web search, or code execution. Permissions and environment — boundaries controlling what tools can read, change, or communicate externally. This distinction prevents common mistakes. For example, a chat session without a code tool cannot execute a program, while Claude Code can run project commands when its environment and permissions allow it. 7.3 Useful strengths Claude is often useful for: explaining unfamiliar code and technical concepts; drafting, refactoring, and documenting code; proposing tests, edge cases, and alternative designs; synthesizing information supplied in the current context; exploring a repository and carrying out multi-step work when tools are available; and translating ambiguous goals into a concrete plan for human review. These are capabilities, not guarantees. Output quality depends on the task, context, model, tools, and verification process. 7.4 Important limitations 7.4.1 Outputs can be wrong Claude can produce plausible but incorrect facts, citations, assumptions, code, or calculations. Verify consequential claims against primary sources and verify code with tests, builds, static analysis, or direct inspection. 7.4.2 Product capabilities vary Web access, code execution, file access, memory, and integrations are not universal. A feature may be unavailable, disabled, permission-gated, or supplied by a third-party host. State the environment when documenting a workflow. 7.4.3 Context is finite Long conversations, large files, and verbose tool output consume context. As context fills, earlier detail may be summarized or receive less attention. Provide focused evidence, keep durable project rules in repository instructions, and begin a fresh session when the task changes substantially. 7.4.4 Current information requires retrieval Model training knowledge is not a substitute for current documentation. For changing APIs, models, prices, regulations, or library behavior, use an enabled retrieval tool and cite an authoritative source. If retrieval is unavailable, label the information as unverified rather than guessing. 7.4.5 Tool use creates real risk An agent with file, shell, browser, or external-service access can change state. Use least privilege, protect secrets, review destructive commands, preserve unrelated work, and require explicit approval for publishing or external actions. 7.5 A verification-centered partnership Divide responsibilities deliberately: Human responsibility Agent contribution Define goals, risk tolerance, and factual constraints Explore, draft, compare, and implement Supply domain and organizational context Surface assumptions and missing information Approve consequential or external actions Run authorized checks and report evidence Judge whether the result is useful and correct Iterate in response to test results and review The agent should show evidence rather than merely announce success. Appropriate evidence might include a passing test, a clean build, a rendered screenshot, a query result, or a primary-source link. 7.6 Exercise: compare environments Choose one task and try it in two Claude environments, such as a chat interface and Claude Code. Record which model and tools are visible. Ask each environment to explain a small local function. Ask whether it can run the function and verify the answer. Compare what each environment can actually inspect or execute. Write down which claims were generated and which were verified. 7.7 Key takeaways Separate the model from the host product, tools, and permissions. Never assume web, file, memory, or execution capabilities are present. Treat fluent output as a candidate result until evidence validates it. Use current primary documentation for changing product behavior. Keep humans responsible for goals, risk, and consequential decisions.

Chapter 8 Prompting Strategies: Ask Better Questions 8.1 The Principle: Clarity Improves Controllability Clear goals, relevant context, examples, constraints, and verification criteria usually make an answer easier to evaluate and refine. Detail is useful only when it is relevant; a longer prompt does not guarantee a better result. Vague request → many plausible interpretations Scoped request → fewer interpretations Scoped request + checks → an answer you can verify 8.2 Structure of a Good Question Many strong requests include these elements: 8.2.1 1. What (What do you want?) Be specific. “Write a function” is vague. “Write a Python function that validates email addresses” is clear. 8.2.2 2. Why (Why do you need it?) Context helps Claude understand intent. “I need to validate emails for a signup form” helps Claude suggest better solutions. 8.2.3 3. How (How should it work?) Constraints and requirements. “It should accept common email formats but reject obvious spam patterns” guides the implementation. 8.2.4 4. Constraints (What are the limits?) Languages, frameworks, performance needs. “Use Python 3.11, must be under 50 lines, no external libraries” keeps answers practical. 8.3 A CLEAR Working Mnemonic The following mnemonic is used in this guide; it is not an Anthropic product feature or an empirical guarantee: Context - What’s the background? Level - What’s your skill level? Example - Can you show an example? Action - What exactly do you want? Result - What’s the expected outcome? 8.4 Comparison: Bad vs. Good Questions 8.4.1 ❌ Bad Question How do I write a function? Problem: Too vague. What kind of function? What language? What should it do? 8.4.2 ✅ Good Question I need a Python function that: - Takes a list of dictionaries with 'date' and 'amount' fields - Groups transactions by month - Returns a dictionary with month as key and total amount as value - Should handle dates in YYYY-MM-DD format - Performance isn't critical, clarity matters more Can you write this with clear variable names? Why it’s better: - Specific about input/output - Clear requirements - Shows format expectations - States preferences (clarity over performance) 8.5 Question Templates You’ll Use Often 8.5.1 Template 1: Code Generation I need to [action] in [language]. Requirements: - [Requirement 1] - [Requirement 2] - [Requirement 3] Input: [example input] Output: [example output] Constraints: [any limits or preferences] 8.5.2 Template 2: Code Explanation I have this code: [paste code] Explain: 1. What does it do? 2. What's the time complexity? 3. What could break? 4. How would you improve it? 8.5.3 Template 3: Debugging I'm trying to [what you're doing]. My code: [paste relevant code] The error: [paste full error message] What I've tried: [what you already attempted] Expected behavior: [what should happen instead] 8.5.4 Template 4: Learning I'm trying to understand [concept]. Context: [what you know already] Can you explain: 1. How it works simply 2. When to use it 3. A practical example 8.6 Prompting Tips & Tricks 8.6.1 ✅ DO: Provide Context I'm building a data pipeline for marketing data. I need to [...] Better than: “I need a function” 8.6.2 ✅ DO: Show Your Attempt I tried this approach: [code] But it's slow. Can you optimize it? Better than: “Make this faster” 8.6.3 ✅ DO: Be Specific About Format Return the result as JSON with keys: 'status', 'data', 'timestamp' Better than: “Return the result” 8.6.4 ✅ DO: Mention Constraints Use only built-in Python libraries (no pandas or numpy) Better than: No constraints 8.6.5 ✅ DO: Ask Follow-up Questions Why is that approach better? Can you show an alternative? How would this scale to 1M rows? Better than: Single question only 8.7 ❌ DON’T: Common Mistakes 8.7.1 ❌ DON’T: Provide Indiscriminate Context Here is a large dump from several unrelated files. What's wrong? Better: In chat, provide the smallest relevant excerpt and enough surrounding context to interpret it. In a coding agent, point to the relevant files and let the agent inspect dependencies as needed. 8.7.2 ❌ DON’T: Vague Requirements Make it better Optimize this Fix the issue Better: “Make it 50% faster while keeping the code readable” 8.7.3 ❌ DON’T: Expect Perfect First Answer Generate this once and I'll use it exactly Better: Expect to iterate and refine 8.7.4 ❌ DON’T: Skip Error Messages It doesn't work Better: Paste the full error including traceback 8.7.5 ❌ DON’T: Ignore Language Versions Write me a regex Better: “Write me a Python 3.11 regex using the re module” 8.8 The Iteration Loop Good prompting is iterative: 1. Ask Claude 2. Review the response 3. Provide feedback ("It needs to handle edge case X") 4. Claude refines 5. Repeat until satisfied Example: - You: “Write a function that validates email” - Claude: [Response] - You: “Good, but also reject emails from temporary services” - Claude: [Improved response] - You: “Perfect, now add error handling” - Claude: [Final version] 8.9 Pro Tip: Use Comments as Instructions When pasting code, add comments showing what you want: def analyze_data(df): # TODO: Filter for active users only # TODO: Group by region # TODO: Calculate total spending per region # TODO: Sort by spending descending pass Claude will often see these comments and implement them! 8.10 Exercise: Write Better Questions Take one of your typical tasks. Write it both ways: Bad version (vague): Write me a Python script Good version (clear): I need a Python script that: - Reads data from CSV file - Filters transactions > $100 - Groups by customer - Exports results to new CSV Format should be: [description of format] I'm using Python 3.10 Notice how much more likely you are to get a useful answer with the good version! 8.11 Key Takeaways ✅ Specific questions get better answers ✅ Include context, examples, and constraints ✅ Use the CLEAR framework ✅ Expect to iterate ✅ Show your attempt, not just the final goal ✅ Be precise about language versions and formats

Chapter 9 Code Best Practices: Generate & Review Code 9.1 The Generate-Review-Refine Workflow Every time you ask Claude for code: GENERATE → REVIEW → REFINE Don’t use first answer immediately. 9.2 Phase 1: Generate Ask Claude for code with full context: Language: Python 3.10 Task: Function to calculate customer lifetime value Requirements: - Input: list of transaction amounts - Output: single float (LTV) - Exclude transactions: < $0, > $10000 (likely errors) - Calculation: sum of valid transactions * 12 months Example: Input: [100, 150, 90, -50, 15000] Output: 3420.0 (sum of [100,150,90] * 12) 9.3 Phase 2: Review - The Quality Checklist After Claude generates code, ask yourself: 9.3.1 ✅ Does It Work? # Copy the code # Run it immediately # Test with examples 9.3.2 ✅ Is It Readable? Good variable names? # GOOD def calculate_customer_ltv(transactions): valid = [t for t in transactions if 0 <= t <= 10000] return sum(valid) * 12 # BAD def f(x): y = [a for a in x if a > 0 and a < 10000] return sum(y) * 12 Clear logic? # GOOD - steps are obvious transactions = read_transactions() valid_transactions = filter_outliers(transactions) ltv = calculate_ltv(valid_transactions) return ltv # BAD - what's happening? return sum([t for t in read_transactions() if 0<t<10000])*12 9.3.3 ✅ Does It Handle Edge Cases? Ask yourself: - What if input is empty? → errors or returns None? - What if input is invalid type? → crashes or handles gracefully? - What if numbers are very large? → overflow issues? - What if data is missing? → NaN/None handling? Example: # WORSE - no error handling def calculate_ltv(transactions): return sum(transactions) * 12 # BETTER - handles edge cases def calculate_ltv(transactions): """Calculate customer lifetime value.""" if not transactions: return None if not isinstance(transactions, (list, tuple)): raise TypeError("transactions must be list or tuple") valid = [ t for t in transactions if isinstance(t, (int, float)) and 0 <= t <= 10000 ] return sum(valid) * 12 if valid else None 9.3.4 ✅ Is It Efficient? Does it make unnecessary loops? Could it use built-in functions? Will it work with large datasets? # INEFFICIENT def clean_data(df): for i in range(len(df)): df.iloc[i, 0] = df.iloc[i, 0].lower() # EFFICIENT def clean_data(df): df[df.columns[0]] = df[df.columns[0]].str.lower() 9.3.5 ✅ Is It Documented? # GOOD def calculate_ltv(transactions: list[float]) -> float: """ Calculate customer lifetime value from transaction history. Args: transactions: List of transaction amounts (floats) Returns: float: Estimated annual value (sum * 12) Raises: TypeError: If transactions is not a list Example: >>> calculate_ltv([100, 150, 90]) 4440.0 """ ... # OKAY def calculate_ltv(transactions): # Returns annual LTV return sum(transactions) * 12 # BAD def f(x): return sum(x) * 12 9.3.6 ✅ Does It Follow Standards? Check your team/project standards: - Naming conventions? (snake_case vs camelCase) - Type hints? - Comments on complex logic? - Docstring style? 9.4 Phase 3: Refine Ask Claude to improve it: Good start! Can you: 1. Add error handling for edge cases 2. Add type hints 3. Add docstring with examples 4. Make it more efficient 5. Add logging for debugging 9.5 Code Quality Checklist Before shipping code, verify: 9.5.1 Functionality ✓ Code runs without errors Handles all expected inputs Produces correct outputs Edge cases handled 9.5.2 Readability ✓ Variable names are clear Logic is straightforward No magic numbers Comments explain “why”, not “what” 9.5.3 Robustness ✓ Error handling present Input validation Graceful failure Appropriate logging 9.5.4 Documentation ✓ Function has docstring Parameters documented Return values documented Examples included 9.5.5 Performance ✓ Appropriate algorithm No unnecessary loops Handles large data No memory leaks 9.5.6 Maintainability ✓ Follows project standards Tests included Dependencies clear Easy to debug 9.6 Common Code Problems Claude Might Miss 9.6.1 ❌ Problem 1: Mutating Input # WRONG - modifies input list! def process(items): items.sort() return items[0] # RIGHT - works on copy def process(items): sorted_items = sorted(items) return sorted_items[0] 9.6.2 ❌ Problem 2: Hardcoded Paths # WRONG - only works on one computer df = pd.read_csv('/Users/name/data.csv') # RIGHT - relative path df = pd.read_csv('../data/customers.csv') 9.6.3 ❌ Problem 3: Missing Imports # Claude writes code using 'os' # But forgot to import it import pandas as pd # missing: import os file_path = os.path.join('data', 'file.csv') # ERROR! 9.6.4 ❌ Problem 4: Silent Failures # WRONG - silently returns None if error def get_value(data, key): try: return data[key] except: pass # What error? Where? Lost forever. # RIGHT - logs or raises def get_value(data, key): try: return data[key] except KeyError as e: raise ValueError(f"Missing required key: {key}") from e 9.7 Asking Claude for Code Review I have this function: [paste code] Code review: 1. Does it work correctly? 2. What edge cases am I missing? 3. How would you improve it? 4. Any performance concerns? 5. Any security concerns? 9.8 Exercise: Review Real Code Take code Claude generated for you: Run it - Does it work? Check readability - Would others understand it? Test edge cases - Does it break? Review documentation - Is it clear? Ask Claude to improve - Iterate Save the before/after. Notice the improvements! 9.9 Key Takeaways ✅ Generate → Review → Refine workflow ✅ Don’t use first answer immediately ✅ Check: Works? Readable? Robust? Documented? ✅ Test edge cases actively ✅ Follow your team’s standards ✅ Ask Claude to iterate

Chapter 10 Advanced Techniques: Power User Features 10.1 When to Use Advanced Techniques You’ve mastered the basics. Now: - ✓ Tackle complex problems - ✓ Work more efficiently - ✓ Get better answers - ✓ Build sophisticated systems These patterns complement Anthropic’s current Claude Code best practices. They are starting points to test, not guarantees of output quality. 10.2 Technique 1: Plan Before Implementation Problem: Claude rushes to answers, misses nuance Solution: Ask for an inspectable plan, assumptions, and verification strategy before implementation. Evaluate the plan itself rather than relying on an unverifiable claim that the model “thought harder.” Problem: Build a data pipeline that: - Reads from 3 sources - Cleans inconsistent data - Validates quality - Outputs to database Before asking for code, ask: "Before you write code, walk me through: 1. Data source details (formats, schemas, sizes) 2. How you'd validate consistency 3. Error handling strategy 4. Performance considerations 5. Testing approach Then show me the implementation." 10.3 Technique 2: Context Stacking Problem: Claude forgets earlier context Solution: Explicitly reference previous decisions Earlier we decided: - Use pandas for data processing - Write to PostgreSQL - Handle nulls by forward-fill - Validate row counts match source Now implement step 4: [your step] Keep these decisions in mind. 10.4 Technique 3: Role-Based Prompting Problem: Generic answers that don’t fit your context Solution: Tell Claude what role to play Review this from the perspective of a senior data scientist at a marketing agency. I'm building a customer segmentation model. The stakeholders are: - VP Marketing (needs actionable segments) - Data Engineering (needs reproducible pipeline) - Analytics (needs SQL-friendly outputs) Design the segmentation approach that satisfies all three. 10.5 Technique 4: Constraint-Based Design Problem: Solutions don’t fit real constraints Solution: State constraints explicitly upfront Design a recommendation system with these constraints: - Python 3.10 (the version pinned in production) - No TensorFlow/PyTorch (not allowed in company) - Must run on company GPU (NVIDIA A100) - Must score 1M items in < 2 seconds - Storage limited to 100GB What's the approach? 10.6 Technique 5: Assumption Surfacing Problem: Claude makes wrong assumptions about your needs Solution: Have Claude list assumptions, then validate "Before you build this, list all your assumptions about: 1. Data shape and size 2. Performance requirements 3. Error tolerance 4. Team skill level 5. Business constraints I'll tell you which are wrong so you adjust." 10.7 Technique 6: Comparative Analysis Problem: One solution might not be best Solution: Ask Claude for multiple approaches "Show me 3 different ways to [task]: Approach A: [description] - Pros: - Cons: Approach B: [description] - Pros: - Cons: Approach C: [description] - Pros: - Cons: Which would you recommend for [specific context]?" 10.8 Technique 7: Systematic Testing Strategy Problem: Incomplete test coverage Solution: Ask Claude to design test strategy first "Design a comprehensive test strategy for [function]: 1. What are the possible inputs? 2. What could go wrong? 3. What edge cases exist? 4. How do you test robustness? 5. How do you test performance? 6. How do you test failure modes? Then write tests for all categories." 10.9 Technique 8: Documentation-First Design Problem: Code without clear purpose Solution: Have Claude write documentation first "Write the documentation for this feature first: Title: [what it does] Purpose: [why it matters] How to use: [examples] Inputs: [types and formats] Outputs: [expected results] Edge cases: [special handling] Performance: [expected runtime] Then implement code that matches this documentation." 10.10 Technique 9: Architectural Review Problem: Missing the big picture Solution: Have Claude diagram/explain architecture "Draw (in ASCII or describe) the architecture for: 1. Data inputs (where from?) 2. Processing stages (what happens when?) 3. Storage (where does it live?) 4. Outputs (where does it go?) 5. Monitoring (how do we know it works?) 6. Failure handling (what if it breaks?) 7. Scaling (what if data grows 100x?) Then show the implementation." 10.11 Technique 10: Iterative Refinement Problem: One pass isn’t perfect Solution: Use feedback loops Round 1: "Give me a basic implementation" [you review] Round 2: "Add error handling for [issues found]" [you review] Round 3: "Optimize for [performance issue]" [you review] Round 4: "Add docs and tests" [you test] Round 5: "Final review - anything missing?" [ready for production] 10.12 Advanced Pattern: Complete System Design Combine techniques for major projects: Step 1: UNDERSTAND "I need to build [system]. Constraints: [list] Team: [size and skills] Timeline: [how long]" Step 2: DESIGN "Before coding, design the architecture. Show: inputs → processing → outputs" Step 3: ASSUMPTIONS "What assumptions are you making? Let me validate them." Step 4: COMPONENTS "Break it into 4-5 key components. For each: purpose, inputs, outputs." Step 5: TESTING "Design the test strategy. What could fail? How do we prevent it?" Step 6: IMPLEMENTATION "Now implement [Component 1] with full docs and tests" Step 7: INTEGRATION "Connect [Component 1] to [Component 2]. Show integration points." Step 8: FINAL REVIEW "Review the complete system. Any performance or robustness issues?" Step 9: DEPLOYMENT "How do we deploy this safely? What monitoring do we need?" 10.13 When to Use Each Technique Situation Use This Simple task, clear requirements Basic prompting Complex problem Multi-step thinking Need consistent context Context stacking Domain-specific needs Role-based prompting Real-world constraints Constraint-based design Unsure of requirements Assumption surfacing Choosing approach Comparative analysis Quality concerns Systematic testing Unclear purpose Documentation first Large system Architectural review 10.14 Asking Claude About Advanced Techniques I'm building [system]. Current challenge: [specific problem] I want to use [technique name] to solve it. Here's my context: [describe situation] Can you: 1. Help me apply [technique] correctly 2. Show me the process 3. Help me think through the problem 4. Suggest what I might be missing 10.15 Exercise: Practice Advanced Techniques Pick one technique and use it for your next project: Chosen technique: [name] Your problem: [description] Apply the technique: [work through steps] Result: [what improved?] Track what changed. Most people find techniques save time and improve quality. 10.16 Key Takeaways ✅ Multi-step thinking = better solutions ✅ Role-based prompting = relevant answers ✅ Constraint design = practical solutions ✅ Comparative analysis = better choices ✅ Architecture first = fewer rewrites ✅ Testing strategy = robust code ✅ Combine techniques for complex work

Chapter 12 Claude Code Hooks: Deterministic Automation 12.1 What hooks are Claude Code hooks are user-defined commands or evaluations that run at specific points in the agent lifecycle. They can format files after edits, block unsafe operations, run checks, send notifications, or add context. Unlike a prompt that asks the model to remember a rule, a command hook provides deterministic control whenever its configured event fires. This chapter is about Claude Code hooks, not React hooks. Product behavior changes over time; consult Anthropic’s current hooks guide and hooks reference before adopting an example. 12.2 When a hook is appropriate Use a hook when all three conditions hold: A lifecycle event can identify when the check should run. A command or structured evaluation can decide the result reliably. Running automatically is safer or more consistent than relying on memory. Good candidates include formatting edited files, rejecting writes to protected paths, checking generated output, or notifying the user that input is required. Do not use a hook for subjective decisions that need rich context unless a prompt- or agent-based hook is explicitly appropriate and its uncertainty is acceptable. 12.3 Core lifecycle pattern Common events include: SessionStart — when a session begins or resumes; UserPromptSubmit — before Claude processes a submitted prompt; PreToolUse — before a matching tool call executes; PostToolUse — after a matching tool call succeeds; Stop — when Claude is preparing to finish; and Notification — when Claude needs attention or permission. The exact event set and schemas are versioned product behavior. Verify event names in the current reference rather than copying an old list into production. Command hooks normally receive JSON on standard input. Their standard output, standard error, exit code, and—in some cases—structured JSON tell Claude Code what happened. An exit code of zero does not automatically grant permission to a tool; the normal permission flow still applies unless the event supports and receives an explicit decision. 12.4 Example: format edited Python files The following project setting illustrates a narrowly scoped post-edit hook: { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "python .claude/hooks/format_python.py" } ] } ] } } The script should read the event JSON from standard input, validate the supplied path, do nothing for non-Python files, and invoke the project’s pinned formatter. Avoid interpolating untrusted paths directly into a shell command. Prefer a small script that parses JSON and passes arguments to a subprocess without a shell. 12.5 Example: protect sensitive paths A PreToolUse hook can inspect an impending edit and block access to paths such as .env, credential stores, or .git/. A robust implementation should: parse the documented JSON field rather than scrape text; canonicalize and validate the path; compare against a small explicit denylist or allowlist; return the documented blocking result; and explain the reason without printing secret contents. Hooks supplement permissions and repository policy; they are not a complete security boundary. A configuration mistake, unmatched tool, indirect command, or future schema change can bypass an incomplete rule. 12.6 Safe design checklist Before enabling a hook: Pin or verify every external command it invokes. Quote paths safely and avoid eval or shell construction from event input. Keep matchers narrow so unrelated tools do not trigger side effects. Make repeated execution idempotent where possible. Bound runtime and output volume. Do not print tokens, environment secrets, or private file contents. Test allow, deny, malformed-input, and missing-dependency cases. Document whether failure blocks work or only reports a warning. Review project-level hooks before running an unfamiliar repository. 12.7 Choosing between instructions, skills, and hooks Mechanism Best use CLAUDE.md or project instructions Durable facts, conventions, and commands Claude should know Skill Reusable, on-demand procedure with instructions and supporting resources Command hook Deterministic action tied to a lifecycle event Prompt/agent hook Judgment-based event evaluation where model uncertainty is acceptable Start with the least complex mechanism that solves the problem. A short project instruction is easier to inspect than a hook; a hook is valuable when reliable automatic enforcement justifies its operational risk. 12.8 Exercise: design before enabling Design a hook on paper for one repeated task: Name the exact lifecycle event and matcher. Specify the JSON fields the handler needs. Define success, warning, and blocking outcomes. List side effects and secrets the handler must not expose. Write test cases before enabling the hook. Compare the configuration with the current official reference. 12.9 Key takeaways Claude Code hooks are lifecycle automation, not React state-management hooks. Use command hooks for narrow, deterministic checks and actions. Treat hook input as untrusted and keep permissions least-privileged. Test failure behavior and idempotency before relying on a hook. Recheck official documentation because event schemas and capabilities evolve.

Chapter 13 Claude Code Skills: Reusable Procedures 13.1 What a skill is A Claude Code skill is a directory whose required SKILL.md file describes a reusable procedure. Claude can load a skill when its description matches the task, or the user can invoke it directly. Skills are useful when the same instructions, checklist, or multi-step workflow would otherwise be pasted into many conversations. Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard and add product-specific features. Review the current Claude Code skills documentation before depending on invocation or frontmatter behavior. 13.2 Where skills live Common locations are: Scope Location Intended use Personal ~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md Available across the user’s projects Project .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md Shared rules for one repository Plugin <plugin>/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md Distributed as part of a plugin Use project scope for procedures that depend on repository-specific commands, paths, or standards. Do not put personal credentials or machine-specific secrets inside a shared skill. 13.3 Minimal structure .claude/ └── skills/ └── summarize-changes/ └── SKILL.md A minimal SKILL.md contains YAML frontmatter and instructions: --- description: Summarize uncommitted changes and flag security, privacy, testing, or deployment risks. Use when reviewing a diff before a commit. --- # Review procedure 1. Inspect repository instructions and Git status. 2. Review source and generated-output diffs separately. 3. Identify secrets, personal data, large files, and unrelated changes. 4. Run the smallest relevant validation. 5. Report evidence, uncertainty, and remaining risks. The directory name normally supplies the command name. The description should state both what the skill does and when it applies; vague descriptions lead to missed or inappropriate activation. 13.4 Progressive disclosure Keep the main skill focused on routing and procedure. Put long examples, schemas, or domain references in supporting files and tell the skill exactly when to read them. model-review/ ├── SKILL.md ├── references/ │ ├── classification.md │ └── regression.md └── scripts/ └── validate_metrics.R This design reduces unnecessary context while keeping important detail available. Supporting scripts should be deterministic, reviewed, and narrowly scoped. 13.5 Methodologically sound data-science skills A skill should encode decisions that remain valid across the intended tasks and surface decisions that depend on context. Avoid hard-coding one universal model, split ratio, imputation rule, or metric. For a model-development skill, require the agent to: Define the prediction target, observation unit, decision use, and costs of errors. Inspect data provenance, sampling, missingness, and temporal structure. Choose a split strategy before fitting transformations; use temporal or grouped splitting when random splitting would leak information. Fit preprocessing only on training data, preferably inside a pipeline. Establish a simple baseline before tuning complex models. Select metrics that match the use case and class distribution. Preserve a held-out test set for final evaluation. Report uncertainty, subgroup behavior, assumptions, and limitations. Save reproducibility information such as seeds, package versions, and data snapshot identifiers. The skill should request missing context instead of silently inventing it. 13.6 Example skill: notebook review --- description: Review a data-science notebook for reproducibility, leakage, methodological validity, privacy, and clear communication. --- # Procedure 1. Read the notebook from top to bottom and identify its analytical objective. 2. Check whether a clean kernel can run all cells in order. 3. Trace data splits and ensure preprocessing is learned from training data only. 4. Check metrics against the decision problem and baseline. 5. Identify secrets, personal data, absolute paths, or uncontrolled downloads. 6. Separate exploratory conclusions from validated findings. 7. Run the notebook only when execution is authorized and dependencies are safe. 8. Report findings by severity with file or cell references. 13.7 Evaluation and maintenance Test a skill with representative prompts, borderline prompts, and prompts where it should not activate. Review whether it: loads at the right time; requests necessary information; follows project safety rules; produces a consistent, useful artifact; runs only authorized tools; and remains understandable to another maintainer. Version skills in Git when they are part of a project. Review them after tool, workflow, or product changes, and remove instructions that duplicate higher priority repository policy. 13.8 Skills are not enforcement A skill supplies instructions and optional resources; it is not a security boundary. Use permissions, protected branches, CI checks, secrets management, and narrowly scoped hooks for controls that must be enforced independently of model behavior. 13.9 Exercise: create one project skill Choose a repeated, bounded procedure such as validating a book build: Define the trigger in one sentence. Write a minimal SKILL.md with expected evidence and stop conditions. Add only the references or scripts the procedure genuinely needs. Test correct activation, non-activation, and a failure case. Ask another reviewer to follow the skill without additional explanation. 13.10 Key takeaways A skill is a scoped directory with a required SKILL.md, not an arbitrary saved-prompt folder. Put repository-specific procedures in project scope and keep secrets out. Encode invariant safeguards; ask for context-dependent methodological choices. Evaluate activation, output quality, safety, and failure behavior. Use permissions, CI, and hooks when instructions alone are insufficient.

Chapter 14 Verification Loops for Agent-Assisted Work 14.1 What Are Quality Loops? Loops are systematic processes that improve work quality over time. First Pass → Review → Feedback → Improvement → Next Pass Three useful levels are: 1. Execution loop — make the smallest checkable unit run. 2. Quality loop — review robustness, clarity, tests, security, and maintainability. 3. Outcome-validation loop — determine whether the result works for the real use case. These levels are conceptual, not fixed schedules. The time and evidence required depend on risk, complexity, reversibility, and the cost of error. 14.2 Loop 1: Execution Loop Purpose: Produce the smallest runnable increment and obtain direct evidence. Cycle: Generate → Test → Refine 14.2.1 The execution-loop process 1. Ask Claude for code ↓ 2. Run it (test immediately) ↓ 3. Does it work? ├─ YES → keep it └─ NO → tell Claude the error ↓ 4. Claude fixes it ↓ 5. Test again (repeat until working) 14.2.2 Execution-loop checklist Generation Phase: - ✓ Provide clear requirements - ✓ Include examples if possible - ✓ Specify constraints (language, libraries) Testing Phase: - ✓ Run the code immediately - ✓ Test with actual data - ✓ Check edge cases Refinement Phase: - ✓ Share exact error messages - ✓ Explain what’s wrong - ✓ Ask for specific fixes 14.2.3 Example: execution loop in action You: "Write a function that validates email addresses" Claude: [Response with regex function] You: [Run function] "Error: It rejects valid emails like test+tag@gmail.com" Claude: [Updates regex to handle plus sign] You: [Run again] "The examples now pass. Add a docstring and property-based tests for edge cases." Claude: [Adds documentation] You: [Final test] "Great, this works!" 14.3 Loop 2: Quality Loop Purpose: Make code production-ready Cycle: Working → Review → Improve → Test 14.3.1 Quality Loop Process Working code ↓ Code review checklist ↓ Ask Claude for improvements ↓ Error handling added ↓ Edge cases handled ↓ Documentation complete ↓ Performance acceptable ↓ Production-ready code 14.3.2 Quality Loop Checklist Error Handling: - ✓ What if input is wrong type? - ✓ What if input is missing? - ✓ What if data is empty? - ✓ Graceful error messages Robustness: - ✓ Edge cases (boundaries, empty input) - ✓ Large inputs (performance) - ✓ Unusual inputs (null, negative, etc) Code Quality: - ✓ Readable variable names - ✓ Clear logic, simple flow - ✓ DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) - ✓ Follows team standards Documentation: - ✓ Function docstring - ✓ Parameters explained - ✓ Return values explained - ✓ Example usage Testing: - ✓ Unit tests included - ✓ Tests cover edge cases - ✓ Tests pass 14.3.3 Example: Quality Loop Working function: def calculate_roi(investment, return_value): profit = return_value - investment roi = (profit / investment) * 100 return roi You ask Claude: "Make this production-ready. Add: 1. Error handling for invalid inputs 2. Docstring 3. Unit tests 4. Handle edge cases (zero investment, negative values)" Claude improves it with: - Input validation - Clear docstring with examples - Type hints - Unit tests - Edge case handling 14.4 Loop 3: Outcome-Validation Loop Purpose: Verify solution solves real problem Cycle: Deploy → Monitor → Collect feedback → Improve 14.4.1 Validation Loop Process Deploy to staging ↓ Collect real usage data ↓ Measure performance/quality ↓ Gather user feedback ↓ Identify issues ↓ Ask Claude to fix ↓ Re-test ↓ Deploy to production 14.4.2 Validation Loop Checklist Pre-Deployment: - ✓ Works in staging environment - ✓ Performance acceptable - ✓ Data looks correct - ✓ Team has reviewed During Testing: - ✓ Monitor for errors - ✓ Track performance metrics - ✓ Get user feedback - ✓ Watch for edge cases Post-Feedback: - ✓ Document issues found - ✓ Prioritize fixes - ✓ Ask Claude to improve - ✓ Re-test improvements Validation Questions: - ✓ Does it solve the original problem? - ✓ Do real users find it useful? - ✓ Does it handle real data well? - ✓ Are there unexpected issues? 14.4.3 Example: Validation Loop Deployed customer segmentation model... Initial real-data validation - Result: Model works but misses 15% of high-value customers - Action: Tell Claude "The model misses high-value customers with unusual purchase patterns" Claude improves feature engineering... Next validation cycle: Re-test - Result: Better, but still has issues - Action: Gather feedback from domain experts Final pre-release cycle - Claude tunes model based on expert feedback - Record remaining limitations and obtain the required release approval - Deploy through the normal controlled process 14.5 Combining All Three Loops EXECUTION LOOP QUALITY LOOP OUTCOME-VALIDATION LOOP Get it working → Make it robust → Verify it solves problem Test immediately Review comprehensively Monitor real world Iterate fast Test edge cases Collect feedback Fix errors quickly Add docs/tests Improve based on use 14.6 Tips for Effective Loops 14.6.1 ✅ Execution-loop tips Run code immediately after Claude generates it Share exact error messages (copy-paste full traceback) Test with real data, not just examples 14.6.2 ✅ Quality Loop Tips Use checklists (helps catch issues) Ask Claude: “What could go wrong here?” Write tests while code is fresh Have Claude add docstrings 14.6.3 ✅ Validation Loop Tips Start with staging/test environment Monitor real usage, not test data Collect specific feedback (“when X happens…”) Document issues for Claude to fix 14.7 Common Mistakes 14.7.1 ❌ Skipping execution-loop testing You: "Write me a function" Claude: [Response] You: Never run it, just use it immediately Problem: Hidden bugs appear in production 14.7.2 ❌ Skipping Quality Loop You: Code works, ship it! Problem: Missing error handling, no docs, fails on edge cases 14.7.3 ❌ Skipping Validation Loop You: Model looks good, deploy to production Problem: Real data behaves differently than test data 14.8 Exercise: Practice Loops Take a small project: 1. Execution Loop: Generate → Test → Fix 2. Quality Loop: Add error handling, documentation, review, and tests 3. Validation Loop: Test with real data, get feedback Record the evidence from each loop. Notice how: - Code loop catches syntax/logic errors fast - Quality review reduces avoidable production risk - Validation loop catches real-world issues 14.9 Key Takeaways ✅ Execution loop = direct evidence that the increment runs ✅ Quality loop = evidence about robustness and maintainability ✅ Outcome-validation loop = evidence about usefulness under realistic conditions ✅ Use all three for best results ✅ Follow the checklists ✅ Test at every stage
