Chapter 16 Model Context Protocol (MCP): Connecting Agents to Data and Tools 16.1 Why this chapter exists Earlier chapters treated tools as something the host application “supplies.” The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the most widely adopted open standard for how those tools, data sources, and reusable prompts get supplied. For a data scientist, MCP is the bridge between a foundation model and the governed tables, models, jobs, and dashboards that already exist. MCP is evolving quickly. This chapter separates stable concepts from version-specific details. Check the MCP documentation and the specification before relying on any wire-level behavior. When this chapter was reviewed (October 2026), the latest protocol version was 2026-07-28. 16.2 The problem MCP solves Without a standard, every pairing of an AI application and a data system needs its own integration. With M AI applications (Claude Code, a Streamlit assistant, a Databricks agent, an IDE) and N systems (Unity Catalog, Jira, Google Drive, an internal API), you face roughly M × N custom connectors. MCP turns this into M + N: each system exposes one MCP server, and each AI application implements one MCP client. Any compliant client can then use any compliant server. A common analogy is USB-C for AI applications: one connector shape, many devices. Interview framing: MCP is a protocol, not a model, framework, or agent. It standardizes how context and capabilities are discovered and invoked. It does not decide which model you use or how the model reasons. 16.3 Core architecture Role What it is Example Host The AI application the user interacts with; it coordinates the model and one or more clients Claude Code, Claude Desktop, VS Code, your own Streamlit app Client A connector inside the host that holds one connection to one server The object Claude Code creates for each configured server Server A program that exposes tools, resources, and prompts Databricks managed SQL server, GitHub server, your own audience-tools server A host creates one client per server. The model never talks to a server directly: the model proposes a tool call, the host routes it through the right client, the server executes it, and the result returns to the model as context. User ──► Host (app + LLM) ├── MCP client ──► MCP server: Databricks SQL ──► SQL warehouse ├── MCP client ──► MCP server: UC functions ──► governed functions └── MCP client ──► MCP server: custom (Apps) ──► Jobs API, models 16.3.1 Two layers Data layer — JSON-RPC 2.0 messages that define discovery, the primitives below, and notifications. Transport layer — how the messages travel: stdio: the host launches the server as a local subprocess and talks over standard input and output. Best for personal, local tools. Streamable HTTP: the server runs remotely and is reached over HTTP, with standard authentication (OAuth is recommended). Best for shared, governed, team-wide servers. An older SSE transport is deprecated. A practical stdio pitfall: never write to stdout from a stdio server (for example with print()), because stdout carries the protocol messages. Log to stderr instead. 16.4 The primitives The primitives are the most important concept to learn. Servers expose three: Primitive Who controls it Purpose Marketing-analytics example Tools The model decides when to call (with host approval) Executable actions with a JSON Schema for inputs audience_overlap(segment_a, segment_b), submit_lookalike_job(seed_table) Resources The application or user decides what to attach Read-only context identified by a URI A table schema, a metric glossary, a campaign brief Prompts The user chooses, often as a slash command Reusable, parameterized templates “Explain this basket-analysis output to a client” Each primitive has list and get or call methods (for example tools/list and tools/call), so a client can discover capabilities at run time instead of having them hard-coded. Clients can also offer capabilities to servers. The main one is elicitation: a server can ask the user for missing input or confirmation through the host. Sampling (a server requesting an LLM completion from the client) is deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28. 16.4.1 What a tool definition looks like A server advertises each tool with a name, a description, and an input schema. Simplified: { "name": "audience_overlap", "description": "Count users in two audience segments and their Jaccard overlap. Use when the user asks how much two audiences overlap.", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "segment_a": {"type": "string", "description": "First segment ID"}, "segment_b": {"type": "string", "description": "Second segment ID"} }, "required": ["segment_a", "segment_b"] } } The description is effectively a prompt. The model chooses tools based on it, so a clear statement of what the tool does and when to use it matters as much as the code. 16.5 MCP compared with related ideas Concept What it is Relationship to MCP Function or tool calling A model API feature: the model emits a structured call MCP standardizes where tool definitions come from and how calls are executed REST API A service interface for programs An MCP server often wraps a REST API with model-friendly names, descriptions, and narrower inputs Skills (Chapter 13) Instructions and procedures loaded into context A skill tells the agent how to do a task; MCP gives it access to systems. They work well together RAG Retrieving documents into context A vector-search MCP server is one way to deliver RAG Agent frameworks Orchestration code (LangGraph, the Agent SDK, Mosaic AI Agent Framework) Frameworks can act as MCP hosts or clients A useful rule: skills encode know-how, MCP servers expose capabilities, and permissions or hooks enforce boundaries. 16.6 Common examples Typical servers you will meet: Developer tools: GitHub (issues, pull requests), Sentry (errors), the local filesystem. Knowledge and collaboration: Notion, Google Drive, Slack, Atlassian. Data platforms: Databricks, BigQuery, Snowflake, Postgres, often with schema browsing and query tools. Documentation: vendor documentation servers that let an agent search current docs instead of relying on training data. In Claude Code, adding servers looks like this (see the Claude Code MCP documentation): # Remote server over HTTP claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp # Local stdio server; everything after -- is the server command claude mcp add --transport stdio audience-tools -- uv run server.py # Share a server with the team through .mcp.json in the repo claude mcp add --transport http shared-sql --scope project https://example.com/mcp claude mcp list # inspect configured servers Project scope writes to .mcp.json, which can reference environment variables such as ${DATABRICKS_TOKEN} so that secrets never enter version control. 16.7 MCP in a Databricks marketing-analytics stack This section maps MCP onto a typical agency setup: Streamlit analytical apps, reusable Databricks jobs (lookalike modeling, audience overlap, basket analysis), and assistants built on Databricks-hosted foundation models. 16.7.1 Three ways Databricks supports MCP Based on the Databricks MCP documentation (reviewed October 2026; most features were in Public Preview): Managed MCP servers: Databricks hosts the server, and Unity Catalog permissions apply automatically. Server URL pattern Use Databricks SQL https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/sql Ad hoc SQL against warehouses Unity Catalog functions https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/functions/{catalog}/{schema}/{function_name} Governed, predefined logic as tools Genie https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/genie/{genie_space_id} Natural-language analytics over a curated Genie space AI Search (vector search) https://<workspace-hostname>/api/2.0/mcp/ai-search/{catalog}/{schema}/{index_name} Retrieval over documents such as briefs and reports External MCP servers registered in Unity Catalog (for example Slack, GitHub, or Google Drive), so access is governed centrally. Custom MCP servers hosted as Databricks Apps, reachable at https://<app-url>/mcp over Streamable HTTP, with access controlled by Databricks Apps permissions. See custom MCP servers. Exact URLs, scopes, and preview status change. Confirm them in your workspace’s documentation before building on them. 16.7.2 Pattern 1: Governed analytics as Unity Catalog functions The lowest-effort, best-governed option is to package your reusable, validated logic as Unity Catalog SQL functions and expose them through the managed functions server. The agent can only run what you defined, under the caller’s permissions. An illustrative audience-overlap function (table and column names are hypothetical): CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION marketing.analytics.audience_overlap( segment_a STRING COMMENT 'First segment ID', segment_b STRING COMMENT 'Second segment ID' ) RETURNS TABLE (size_a BIGINT, size_b BIGINT, overlap BIGINT, jaccard DOUBLE) COMMENT 'Sizes of two audience segments, their shared users, and Jaccard overlap. Use for audience-overlap questions.' RETURN WITH a AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM marketing.analytics.segment_members WHERE segment_id = segment_a ), b AS ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM marketing.analytics.segment_members WHERE segment_id = segment_b ), counts AS ( SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a) AS size_a, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM b) AS size_b, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a JOIN b USING (user_id)) AS overlap ) SELECT size_a, size_b, overlap, try_divide(overlap, size_a + size_b - overlap) AS jaccard FROM counts; The function and parameter comments become the tool description that the model reads. The same pattern fits basket analysis, for example top_associations(category, min_support) returning precomputed support, confidence, and lift from a table that a scheduled job refreshes. Why this is a strong default: The logic is reviewed once and reused by every app and agent. Unity Catalog lineage, permissions, and auditing apply. The model cannot invent a different overlap definition from one run to the next. 16.7.3 Pattern 2: A custom server for long-running jobs Lookalike modeling is not a quick query. It trains or scores a model over large data and can run for minutes or hours. Do not make the model wait on a synchronous tool call. Instead, expose a small custom server with job-shaped tools: submit_lookalike_job(seed_audience_id, expansion_pct) triggers an existing, parameterized Databricks Job and returns a run_id; get_job_status(run_id) reports state and, when finished, output table names and validation metrics; describe_lookalike_output(run_id) summarizes the audience size, score distribution, and holdout performance recorded by the job. A minimal local sketch using the official Python SDK (install with uv add "mcp[cli]"). This is an instructional example, not tested production code. In practice the tools would call the Databricks Jobs API through the Databricks SDK: import logging from mcp.server import MCPServer logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) # stderr; never print() in stdio servers logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) mcp = MCPServer("audience-tools") ALLOWED_EXPANSION = {1, 3, 5, 10} # percentages the job was validated for @mcp.tool() def submit_lookalike_job(seed_audience_id: str, expansion_pct: int) -> str: """Start the validated lookalike-modeling Databricks Job for a seed audience. Use only when the user explicitly asks to build a lookalike audience. Returns a run ID; call get_job_status to follow progress. Args: seed_audience_id: Registered seed audience ID, for example "aud_123". expansion_pct: Target audience size as a percent of the reference population. One of 1, 3, 5, or 10. """ if expansion_pct not in ALLOWED_EXPANSION: return f"expansion_pct must be one of {sorted(ALLOWED_EXPANSION)}." logger.info("Submitting lookalike job for %s", seed_audience_id) run_id = trigger_databricks_job(seed_audience_id, expansion_pct) # your wrapper return f"Submitted. run_id={run_id}" @mcp.tool() def get_job_status(run_id: str) -> str: """Return the state of a lookalike job run and, if finished, its outputs.""" return fetch_run_summary(run_id) # your wrapper around the Jobs API if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run(transport="stdio") # use Streamable HTTP when hosting on Databricks Apps Design choices worth noting: The server calls an existing, versioned job. It does not let the model write modeling code at run time. Inputs are narrow and validated (an allow-list of expansion sizes) rather than free-form. The tool description says when not to call it, because submitting a job costs money. Outputs include validation evidence recorded by the job, so the assistant reports holdout metrics instead of guessing quality. 16.7.4 Pattern 3: An AI-assisted Streamlit app as an MCP host Your Streamlit app can be the host. Its loop is: The user asks a question, for example “How much do our sports-fans and new-parents segments overlap, and what do they buy together?” The app sends the conversation and the MCP tool list to a Databricks foundation-model serving endpoint. The model returns tool calls (audience_overlap, top_associations). The app’s MCP client executes them against the managed or custom servers, using the signed-in user’s identity where possible (on-behalf-of-user authentication) so Unity Catalog permissions apply per user. Results go back to the model, which writes the explanation, while the app renders the actual numbers in tables and charts from the tool output. Rendering numbers from tool results, not from the model’s prose, is a simple and important guard against hallucinated metrics. Databricks also provides client helpers for connecting agent code to its MCP servers. Follow Use MCP servers in agents for the currently supported library and authentication pattern rather than copying older snippets. 16.7.5 Pattern 4: Coding agents connected to the workspace Connecting Claude Code to the managed Databricks SQL server lets a coding agent inspect schemas and run read-only exploratory queries while you build a job or app. Point it at a development catalog, prefer a role with read-only access, and treat its query results as exploration, not validated analysis. 16.8 Choosing the right integration Need Prefer Stable, reusable metric or analysis Unity Catalog function via the managed server Business users asking questions of curated tables Genie space via the managed server Search over briefs, decks, or research Vector (AI) Search via the managed server Long-running or multi-step workflows (lookalike, scoring) Custom server on Databricks Apps wrapping existing Jobs One-off personal automation on a laptop Local stdio server A fixed pipeline with no model in the loop No MCP; a scheduled Databricks Job is simpler MCP adds value when a model must choose among capabilities at run time. If the sequence of steps is fixed, ordinary code or orchestration is simpler, cheaper, and easier to test. 16.9 Security, governance, and failure modes MCP servers give a model real access, so treat them as production integrations. Least privilege. Use dedicated service principals or on-behalf-of-user authentication, restrict servers to the catalogs and schemas they need, and prefer read-only access for exploration. Prompt injection. Content returned by a tool (documents, web pages, free-text table fields) can contain instructions. Treat tool output as data, and keep humans approving actions that write, spend, or send. Trust in third-party servers. A server runs code and sees your data. Install only from trusted publishers, pin versions, and review what each tool can do. Secrets. Keep tokens in environment variables or secret scopes, never in .mcp.json, notebooks, or prompts. Too many tools. Dozens of overlapping tools confuse tool selection and consume context. Expose a small set of well-described, task-shaped tools. Privacy. Audience data can be personal data. Return aggregates, enforce minimum cell sizes, and avoid passing user-level identifiers to a model unless that use is approved. Cost. Tools that trigger clusters or jobs should require confirmation and report expected cost or runtime. Version drift. The protocol, SDKs, and vendor servers change. Pin versions and recheck documentation when something breaks. As with skills, MCP is not itself a security boundary. Enforcement belongs in Unity Catalog permissions, Apps permissions, host approval settings, and hooks. 16.10 Exercise: expose one analysis as a governed tool Pick one analysis you repeat often, such as audience overlap. Write it as a Unity Catalog SQL function with clear function and parameter comments. Test it directly in SQL with known segments, including empty and identical segments. Connect a host (Claude Code or a small Streamlit prototype) to the managed functions server for that function. Ask questions that should trigger the tool, questions that should not, and an ambiguous question. Record whether tool selection and answers were correct. Check that numbers in the final answer match the tool output exactly. 16.11 Key takeaways MCP is an open protocol that lets any compliant AI application use any compliant data source or tool, turning M × N integrations into M + N. Hosts contain clients; each client connects to one server; servers expose tools, resources, and prompts. Use stdio for local, personal servers and Streamable HTTP for shared, remote, governed servers. On Databricks, start with managed servers and Unity Catalog functions for reusable logic, and add a custom server on Databricks Apps for job-shaped workflows such as lookalike modeling. Tool descriptions are prompts: say what a tool does, when to use it, and when not to. Apply least privilege, guard against prompt injection, protect personal data, and render reported numbers from tool output. 16.12 References MCP architecture overview MCP specification Build an MCP server (official quickstart) Claude Code: connect tools via MCP Databricks: MCP on Databricks Databricks: managed MCP servers Databricks: custom MCP servers on Databricks Apps

Chapter 17 Context Engineering and Harness Engineering 17.1 Why these two terms matter Earlier chapters covered prompting, verification loops, hooks, skills, and MCP as separate techniques. Two newer terms give those techniques a common frame: Context engineering asks: which tokens should the model see at this step? It covers instructions, retrieved data, tool definitions, tool outputs, conversation history, and memory. Harness engineering asks: what system around the model makes it reliable over many steps? It covers the agent loop, tools, sandbox, state files, hooks, permissions, tests, and evaluation. Both terms are young, and their boundaries are still debated. This chapter separates three kinds of claim: concepts that are likely to last, vendor practices and features that change quickly, and evidence. The evidence is labeled by strength throughout. Source labels used in this chapter [Vendor]: an organization reporting on its own product or results. [Secondary]: the original could not be read; the claim comes from a mirror, summary, or aggregator. [Unverified]: no primary source was found. Product names, API identifiers, and preview status are as of October 2026. 17.2 Where the terms came from 17.2.1 Context engineering (mid-2025) The term spread through a cluster of posts in June and July 2025. No single person has a verified claim to coining it, so “popularized by” is the accurate phrasing. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke described it as “the art of providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM” (June 2025, quoted by Simon Willison). Harrison Chase of LangChain defined it as building dynamic systems that give the model “the right information and tools in the right format,” and credited earlier practitioners (LangChain). Andrej Karpathy called it “the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step.” He compared the model to a CPU and the context window to its RAM (June 2025, quoted by Simon Willison). Drew Breunig named common ways long contexts fail (How contexts fail; How to fix your context). Manus published lessons from running a production agent (Manus, July 2025). Anthropic’s engineering guide (29 September 2025) gave the most-cited definition: strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during LLM inference (Anthropic). 17.2.2 Harness engineering (early 2026) “Harness” and “scaffold” already meant the code around a model. The phrase harness engineering became common in early 2026. Phil Schmid (January 2026) described the agent harness as the infrastructure that wraps a model to manage long-running tasks, and said it is not the agent itself. He extended Karpathy’s analogy: model = CPU, context = RAM, harness = operating system, agent = application (philschmid.de). Mitchell Hashimoto (February 2026) gave the most practical definition: whenever an agent makes a mistake, engineer a fix so it never makes that mistake again. His fixes were updates to AGENTS.md plus small, purpose-built scripts (mitchellh.com). OpenAI published “Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world” (February 2026). It describes a team that designs the environment while agents write the code (OpenAI). [Secondary]: the page could not be read for this chapter. Its widely repeated figures (code volume, team size, number of pull requests) are therefore not reproduced here. LangChain summarized the idea as “Agent = Model + Harness” (LangChain, March 2026). Birgitta Böckeler’s article on martinfowler.com (April 2026) reframed harness engineering for teams that use coding agents (martinfowler.com). Anthropic documented harness patterns for long-running agents (November 2025; March 2026) [Vendor]. These definitions emphasize different things. Hashimoto’s is incremental, OpenAI’s is organizational, Schmid’s and LangChain’s are architectural, and Böckeler’s treats the harness as a control system. 17.3 How prompt, context, and harness relate Layer Question it answers Typical artifacts Prompt engineering How should the instruction be worded? System prompt, few-shot examples Context engineering Which tokens should the model see at this step? Retrieval, tool selection, compaction, memory files, sub-agent summaries Harness engineering What system makes the model reliable over many steps? Agent loop, sandbox, hooks, tests and linters, evaluator agents, state logs, permissions LangChain calls prompt engineering “a subset of context engineering,” and Anthropic calls context engineering its “natural progression.” Treat the chain prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness as a teaching heuristic, not a settled taxonomy: it appears mostly in explainers, not in primary lab writing. The more precise statement is that the harness contains context management, but it also includes deterministic machinery, such as linters, sandboxes, and permission checks. That machinery affects the model only when its output is fed back into the context. Is it just a rebrand? In part. Retrieval, summarization, and RAG all predate the label, and some experienced developers dismiss the term as rebranded prompt engineering (Addy Osmani). What is new is treating these techniques as one budgeted design problem for multi-step agents, which a prompt-only view hides. 17.4 Context engineering 17.4.1 Context is a finite attention budget The founding premise is that more context can make results worse. Anthropic describes a finite “attention budget” and names context rot: recall falls as the token count grows. The goal it sets is “the smallest set of high-signal tokens” that makes the desired outcome likely. Evidence: Lost in the middle. Accuracy was highest when the relevant information sat at the beginning or end of a long input, and worse in the middle (Liu et al., arXiv 2307.03172). Context rot. Across 18 models, performance degraded as input length grew, often unevenly (Chroma, July 2025). [Vendor]: Chroma sells retrieval infrastructure, and the study is not peer reviewed. A practical consequence: a larger advertised context window is a capacity limit, not a promise that the model will use every token equally well. 17.4.2 Four ways context fails Breunig’s taxonomy pairs each failure with a fix. The examples he cites are secondhand and were not checked against the original papers for this chapter. Failure What happens Typical fix Poisoning A hallucination or error enters context and is reused as if true Validate before writing to memory; prune; quarantine Distraction A long history crowds out the task; the agent repeats past actions Summarize or compact; start fresh with a handoff note Confusion Irrelevant tools or documents degrade choices Load fewer tools; retrieve selectively Clash New information contradicts earlier context Remove stale content; keep one source of truth 17.4.3 Four families of technique: write, select, compress, isolate LangChain groups the techniques into four families (LangChain). Write: persist state outside the window. Scratchpads, progress notes, and to-do files let an agent recover after its history is trimmed. Manus has the agent rewrite a todo.md so its goals stay at the end of the context, a direct counter to lost-in-the-middle. Select: retrieve just in time. Keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, table names, saved queries) and load content only when needed. Claude Code combines an up-front CLAUDE.md with on-demand file search. Selection applies to tools too: a smaller, relevant toolset reduces confusion. Compress: summarize or prune. Compaction replaces old history with a summary that keeps decisions, open issues, and key details, and drops redundant tool output. Isolate: give sub-tasks clean windows. A sub-agent explores in its own context and returns a short summary (Anthropic suggests roughly 1,000 to 2,000 tokens). Isolation costs extra tokens, and some practitioners argue that splitting work across agents fragments shared understanding. Choose it for parallel, separable work, not by default. Supporting guidance from the Anthropic guide: Write system prompts at the “right altitude”: specific enough to guide behavior, but heuristic rather than a brittle list of rules. Use a few diverse, canonical examples rather than every edge case. Make tools self-contained, robust to errors, and clearly distinct from one another. Return compact tool outputs, not raw dumps. 17.4.4 Cost: the overlooked dimension Agents read far more tokens than they write. Manus reports a ratio of roughly 100 input tokens per output token and calls the KV-cache hit rate the most important production metric [Vendor]. Cached input tokens are much cheaper than uncached ones, which leads to rules such as: keep the prompt prefix stable (a timestamp at the top breaks the cache); append to the context rather than editing earlier turns; serialize JSON deterministically; and disable tools by masking them rather than removing their definitions. These rules conflict with compaction and dynamic tool removal, which invalidate the cache. Good designs compress rarely and in large steps rather than continuously. Manus also advises leaving failed attempts in context so the model avoids repeating them, which seems to contradict “poisoning.” One reasonable reconciliation (the author’s judgment): observed error messages are useful feedback, while unverified claims stored as facts are harmful. 17.4.5 Context features are becoming platform features Vendors now ship these techniques as features, for example Anthropic’s context editing, memory tool, server-side compaction, and the progressive disclosure built into Agent Skills (Chapter 13). Learn the four families. The API names will change, but the families will still apply. 17.5 Harness engineering 17.5.1 What is in a harness A short working definition: the harness is everything except the model weights. LangChain’s list includes system prompts; tools, skills, and MCP servers (Chapter 16); infrastructure such as a filesystem, sandbox, or browser; orchestration such as sub-agents and model routing; and hooks or middleware for deterministic steps (LangChain). It helps to separate: the builder harness: the product runtime (Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, Codex, LangChain Deep Agents, a custom agent); and the user harness: what your team adds on top, such as AGENTS.md, specs, tests, linters, hooks, permissions, and CI. Most data scientists work mainly on the user harness, or build a small builder harness inside an application. 17.5.2 Guides and sensors Böckeler classifies harness controls on two axes (martinfowler.com): Computational (deterministic, cheap, reliable) Inferential (model-based, slower, non-deterministic) Guides (before the agent acts) Templates, schemas, scaffolding scripts, type definitions AGENTS.md, specs, feature lists, skills Sensors (after the agent acts) Tests, linters, type checks, schema validation, data-quality checks AI code review, LLM judges, evaluator agents Prefer computational sensors wherever they can answer the question, and use inferential ones for judgments that code cannot make. Böckeler also notes the limits: tests do not catch a misdiagnosed problem, over-engineering, or a misunderstood instruction. 17.5.3 Each pattern fixes a named failure Recurring failure Harness response Source Declares success too early Feature list where every item starts “failing”; checklist before exit; stop hooks that require evidence Anthropic (Nov 2025), LangChain [Vendor] Tries to do everything at once Work on one feature per session; commit after each Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] Edits tests to pass Explicit rule against changing tests; protected test files; CI Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] Loses track over long runs Progress log, setup script, descriptive commits, handoff notes Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] Praises its own mediocre work A separate evaluator agent that exercises the result Anthropic (Mar 2026) [Vendor] Repeats the same failing edit Loop detection that interrupts the agent LangChain (Feb 2026) [Vendor] Repeats a known mistake Add a rule to AGENTS.md or a deterministic check Hashimoto (Feb 2026) Documentation is part of the harness, and long documents rot. Several practitioners, OpenAI reportedly among them [Secondary], replaced one large instruction file with a short index that points to focused documents. This is the same idea as progressive disclosure in skills and just-in-time retrieval. Security gaps. The primary harness posts reviewed say little about permissions, sandboxing, secret handling, or prompt injection through tool outputs. Treat these as first-class harness components anyway: apply least privilege, require human approval for actions that write, spend, or send, and keep secrets out of context (see Chapters 12 and 16). 17.5.4 The thin-harness debate Rich Sutton’s “Bitter Lesson” argues that general methods that scale with compute eventually beat hand-built cleverness. Applied to agents, it raises the question of whether harness logic is a temporary crutch. Thin-harness view. Anthropic writes that every harness component “encodes an assumption about what the model can’t do on its own.” When a stronger model arrived, it removed parts of its own harness (Anthropic, March 2026) [Vendor]. Schmid recommends harnesses that make yesterday’s clever logic easy to delete. Harness-matters view. With the model held fixed, LangChain changed only its harness and raised its Terminal-Bench 2.0 score from 52.8% to 66.5% (LangChain) [Vendor]. A May 2026 position paper argues that harness-induced variance can exceed model-induced variance and can reverse model rankings (arXiv 2605.23950); it is an argument, not a controlled meta-analysis. The two views are compatible. Specific components (elaborate prompts, rigid step structures, large tool collections) are absorbed as models improve. The need for an environment, verification, persistent state, and permissions remains. Practical implication: a leaderboard score measures a model–harness pair. When you compare models for your own application, hold the harness constant, and when you change the harness, hold the model constant. 17.5.5 Evaluation is a harness too Anthropic’s guide to agent evaluation distinguishes the evaluation harness from the agent harness and defines tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, and outcomes (Anthropic, January 2026): Graders can be code-based (tests, exact match, schema checks), model-based (rubrics, pairwise comparison), or human (expert review). Grade outcomes, not paths. Judge what the agent produced, but keep transcripts for debugging and for spotting reward hacking, such as an agent editing the tests it is graded on. pass@k versus pass^k. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds; pass^k is the chance that all k succeed. For a production tool that users run repeatedly, pass^k is the more honest reliability measure. For a statistician, this is familiar ground: define the estimand (task success), use repeated trials to estimate variance, and avoid grading on the training set (tasks the harness was tuned on). 17.6 Applying both to Databricks analytics apps The design principle that follows from the evidence is: The model chooses and explains; governed engines compute; sensors verify. This is the author’s synthesis rather than an official Databricks rule, but each part has support in the sources above. 17.6.1 Metadata is the highest-return context Text-to-SQL research suggests that semantic context often matters more than which frontier model you pick: Adding a 4 KB semantic-layer document raised accuracy on 100 retail questions from about 46–51% to about 68–69% across three frontier models, and the differences between models were not statistically significant in either condition (arXiv 2604.25149). This is a single study on one domain. On the BIRD benchmark, better column descriptions improved accuracy, although ambiguous columns still needed expert input (arXiv 2408.04691). Automatically profiled metadata helped one team reach the top of the BIRD leaderboard (arXiv 2505.19988). Databricks’ own Genie guidance is a context-engineering playbook (Genie best practices): Rely on clear Unity Catalog table and column names and descriptions. Start with a small number of tables (the docs suggest five or fewer). Prefer SQL expressions for metrics, filters, and dimensions, then example SQL for complex questions, and use plain-text instructions only as a last resort. Unity Catalog metric views define each measure once (reach, overlap rate, lift, support, confidence) so that every app and agent computes it the same way. For an analytics team, this is good news: the highest-return work is data governance work you may already own. Column comments, metric definitions, and verified example queries now have a new consumer. 17.6.2 Mapping to the three workloads Workload Context engineering Harness engineering Evaluation Streamlit analytical apps on Databricks Apps Send aggregates (top-N, group-bys, summary statistics), not audience-level rows. Keep few tables in scope. Keep a stable system-prompt prefix On-behalf-of-user auth so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply per user. The model proposes SQL or tool parameters; tables and charts render from the result DataFrame, not from model text A code check that every number in the narrative appears in the result table; an LLM judge for groundedness Reusable jobs (lookalike, audience overlap, basket analysis) Unity Catalog comments on seed, segment, and transaction tables; metric views for overlap, lift, support, and confidence; a few verified example queries for tricky logic such as fiscal calendars Expose validated logic as Unity Catalog functions or job-triggering tools via MCP. For coding agents that maintain the job code, a short AGENTS.md map plus tests act as guides and sensors Compare results with known gold outputs; measure pass^k across repeated runs; protect unit tests from agent edits AI-assisted apps on Databricks foundation models (Genie, Agent Bricks, custom agents) Follow the Genie order of instruction types; retrieve methodology documents just in time with AI Search rather than preloading them Gateway quotas and budgets; guardrails; durable memory only for state that must persist. Inference logging stores whatever enters context, so keep personal data out Genie benchmarks; MLflow GenAI evaluation with code scorers and judges; labeled cases where the app should ask for clarification or refuse Relevant Databricks references: Databricks Apps authorization, managed MCP servers (Public Preview), and the Foundation Model APIs supported models page. Product names change often: Genie spaces are now called Genie Agents, Vector Search is now AI Search, and AI Gateway is now Unity Gateway. Check each docs page’s preview banner before relying on a feature. 17.6.3 Three cautions for marketing data Schema confusion is tool confusion. Too many tables in scope degrade text-to-SQL the same way too many tools degrade tool choice. Curate. Client data in prompts is both a privacy risk and a cost. Aggregate first, enforce minimum cell sizes, and use per-user authorization. Do not let the assistant grade its own narrative. A deterministic check against the result table is cheaper and more reliable than asking a model whether its lift or overlap summary is correct. 17.7 A minimal sketch: the number-check sensor This illustrative check implements the third caution. It is an instructional example, not tested production code, and the regular expression handles only simple number formats. import re import pandas as pd def numbers_in_text(text: str) -> set[float]: """Extract plain numbers such as 12, 3.5, 1,200 or 45% from narrative text.""" tokens = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text) return {round(float(t.replace(",", "")), 2) for t in tokens} def unsupported_numbers(narrative: str, result: pd.DataFrame) -> set[float]: """Return numbers in the narrative that do not appear in the result table.""" numeric = result.select_dtypes("number").to_numpy().ravel() allowed = {round(float(x), 2) for x in numeric} allowed |= {round(float(x) * 100, 2) for x in numeric} # shares shown as % return numbers_in_text(narrative) - allowed result = pd.DataFrame({"segment": ["A", "B"], "overlap_rate": [0.18, 0.07]}) narrative = "Segment A overlaps 18% with the seed audience, versus 9% for B." print(unsupported_numbers(narrative, result)) # {9.0} -> flag for review In a harness, this check runs after the model writes its summary. If it finds unsupported numbers, the app either asks the model to revise using only the table or shows the table without the narrative. 17.8 Exercise: audit one AI-assisted app Choose an existing assistant or prototype and answer: Context inventory. List everything in the context window on a typical request: system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved text, history. Estimate tokens for each. What could be removed or loaded just in time? Failure mapping. Find one real failure and classify it as poisoning, distraction, confusion, or clash, or as a harness failure such as premature success or missing verification. One guide, one sensor. Add one guide (a metric definition, example query, or AGENTS.md rule) and one computational sensor (a schema check, number check, or test). Measure. Build 20 to 30 representative questions with known answers. Run each several times and report pass^k before and after your change, holding the model constant. 17.9 Key takeaways Context engineering decides what the model sees at each step; harness engineering builds the system that makes many steps reliable. Treat prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness as a useful heuristic, not an official taxonomy; the harness also includes deterministic parts that never enter the context. Context is a finite attention budget: more tokens can reduce quality. Use the four families—write, select, compress, isolate—and watch the cost trade-off with caching. Organize harness controls as guides and sensors, and prefer deterministic sensors where possible. Each harness component should fix a named failure. Benchmarks measure a model–harness pair. Hold one fixed when you evaluate the other, and report pass^k for reliability. On Databricks, governed metadata is the best context, deterministic functions and jobs are the best tools, and numbers should come from query results. Expect specific techniques and API names to expire; the separation of concerns is the durable lesson. 17.10 References Context engineering Anthropic: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Sep 2025) LangChain: The rise of context engineering (Jun 2025) LangChain: Context engineering for agents (Jul 2025) Simon Willison: Context engineering (Jun 2025) Phil Schmid: The new skill in AI is not prompting, it’s context engineering (Jun 2025) Drew Breunig: How long contexts fail (Jun 2025) Drew Breunig: How to fix your context (Jun 2025) Manus: Context engineering for AI agents (Jul 2025) Chroma: Context rot (Jul 2025) Liu et al.: Lost in the middle (2023) Harness engineering Phil Schmid: The importance of agent harness in 2026 (Jan 2026) Mitchell Hashimoto: My AI adoption journey (Feb 2026) OpenAI: Harness engineering (Feb 2026) LangChain: Improving deep agents with harness engineering (Feb 2026) LangChain: The anatomy of an agent harness (Mar 2026) Birgitta Böckeler: Harness engineering (martinfowler.com, Apr 2026) Anthropic: Effective harnesses for long-running agents (Nov 2025) Anthropic: Harness design for long-running application development (Mar 2026) Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents (Jan 2026) arXiv 2605.23950: position paper on harness-induced variance (May 2026) Databricks and text-to-SQL Databricks: Genie best practices Databricks: Unity Catalog metric views Databricks: MLflow GenAI evaluation Databricks: Apps authorization arXiv 2604.25149: semantic layer and text-to-SQL accuracy (Apr 2026) arXiv 2408.04691: column descriptions on BIRD arXiv 2505.19988: automatic metadata for text-to-SQL

Chapter 18 AI Models in Marketing Analytics 18.1 Introduction Marketing analytics has used statistical and machine-learning models for decades. Response models, customer segmentation, propensity scores, and marketing mix models were standard well before large language models existed. What has changed is the range of tasks that models can now take on. Predictive models score audiences. Causal models estimate what spend actually caused. Generative models write copy, summarize research, and turn questions into SQL. Agents chain these steps together and call governed tools. This chapter maps where each kind of model fits in day-to-day marketing analytics work, especially in an agency setting that serves many clients, markets, and data sources. It ties the earlier chapters to the domain: prompting and verification (Chapters 8 and 14), MCP (Chapter 16), and context and harness engineering (Chapter 17). Two principles run through the chapter: Use the right model family for the question. A language model is not a substitute for a causal design, and a propensity model does not estimate incrementality. Many costly mistakes in marketing analytics come from answering a causal question with a predictive tool. The model chooses and explains; governed engines compute. Generative AI is most useful as an interface to validated analyses, not as the source of the numbers. Measurement theory (marketing mix modeling, attribution, experimentation, and segmentation) is covered in depth in the companion Marketing Analytics book. This chapter focuses on how AI models are used across that work. 18.2 A map of AI model families in marketing Four families of models solve different kinds of problems: predictive (classification, regression, ranking), causal (experiments, quasi-experiments, econometric models), generative (language, image, and multimodal models), and agentic systems that combine models with tools. For each, this section will cover the typical marketing questions it answers, the data it needs, and the question it cannot answer on its own. 18.3 Audience and customer modeling This section covers segmentation, lookalike and propensity modeling, customer lifetime value, and churn. It will also discuss where foundation models and embeddings add value, for example by turning unstructured behavioral or text data into features. The recurring risks are leakage from post-outcome features, seed-audience bias, and treating a high propensity score as proof of incrementality. Chapter 19 treats lookalike modeling as positive-unlabeled learning and covers two-tower embeddings and typed decision models in depth. 18.4 Measurement, attribution, and incrementality This section explains how AI fits around measurement without replacing causal identification. Topics include marketing mix models (for example the open-source Meridian and Robyn projects), multi-touch attribution and its limits, geo and holdout experiments, and how language models can help explain results to clients while the estimates themselves come from validated models. 18.5 Media planning, reach, and audience overlap This section covers budget allocation and scenario planning, reach and frequency estimation, and audience overlap across platforms and segments. It discusses optimization on top of response curves and how an assistant can expose these analyses as governed tools rather than ad hoc calculations. 18.6 Basket analysis and recommendations This section covers market basket analysis (support, confidence, and lift), product affinity, and recommendation systems. It also covers embedding-based approaches and how to explain affinity results in plain language without overstating causality. 18.7 Generative AI for content and creative This section covers copy and creative variation, localization across markets, brief generation, and creative pre-testing. It addresses brand safety, factual claims in ads, intellectual-property and disclosure considerations, and why creative variants still need a proper experiment to show which one works. 18.8 Voice of the customer: text, reviews, and social This section covers using language models to classify, summarize, and extract themes from reviews, survey open-ends, call transcripts, and social posts. It compares zero-shot LLM labeling with traditional supervised classifiers and explains how to validate LLM labels against a human-coded sample before reporting the results. 18.9 AI-assisted analytics workflows This section covers analytics copilots and text-to-SQL assistants (such as Databricks Genie), automated reporting and insight narration, and Streamlit apps built on foundation models. It applies the metadata-first, numbers-from- the-engine design from Chapter 17. 18.10 Agents in marketing operations This section covers multi-step agents that monitor campaign performance, detect anomalies, prepare client reports, or trigger reusable jobs such as lookalike builds. It addresses permissions, human approval for actions that spend or publish, and auditability. 18.11 Data foundations and privacy This section covers first-party data, identity resolution, data clean rooms, consent, and regional privacy regulation. It explains why aggregation, minimum cell sizes, and per-user authorization matter more once client data can flow into model context and logs. 18.12 Evaluation and governance This section covers how to evaluate each model family: offline metrics for predictive models, validity checks for causal estimates, human-validated benchmarks for generative tasks, and repeated-run reliability (pass^k) for assistants and agents. It also covers fairness in targeting, monitoring for drift, and documenting model limits for clients. 18.13 Interview takeaways This section will summarize how to explain these choices in an interview: which model family fits a stated business question, how to defend a measurement approach, and how to describe the safe use of generative AI on client data. 18.14 Key takeaways Marketing analytics uses four model families: predictive, causal, generative, and agentic. Match the family to the question. Predictive accuracy is not incrementality; causal questions need causal designs. Generative AI is strongest as an interface to validated analyses and as a tool for unstructured text and creative work. Governed metadata, deterministic tools, privacy controls, and evaluation turn AI prototypes into dependable client-facing products.

Chapter 19 Classification and Lookalike Modeling: PU Learning, Two-Tower Networks, and Typed Decision Models 19.1 Introduction Marketing data science classifies constantly. It scores leads, routes inquiries, labels reviews, and finds new customers who resemble existing ones. Three developments have changed how this work can be done: Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning gives lookalike modeling a principled footing when advertisers know their positives (the seed audience) but have no confirmed negatives. The wider population is not negative. It is unlabeled: it contains future customers, customers of competitors, and people who simply were never observed. Treating all unlabeled records as negatives is the common shortcut. It biases probability estimates downward because the “negatives” contain hidden positives. 19.3.2 The key assumption and a useful result Most PU methods assume that labeled positives are a random sample of all positives, often called selected completely at random (SCAR). Under SCAR, Elkan and Noto (2008) showed that: \[ P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{P(s = 1 \mid x)}{c}, \qquad c = P(s = 1 \mid y = 1), \] where \(s = 1\) means “in the seed” and \(y = 1\) means “truly positive.” Two practical consequences follow: Ranking is unchanged. Dividing by a constant does not change the order of scores. If you only need the top-k users, the naive seed-versus-rest classifier already produces the same ranking as the PU-corrected one under SCAR. Probabilities and audience sizes change. If you need calibrated probabilities, expected conversions, or an estimate of how many positives exist in the population, you must estimate \(c\). The SCAR assumption is often doubtful in marketing. Seed audiences come from past campaigns, specific channels, or loyalty programs, so they are rarely a random sample of all potential customers. When selection depends on features, the naive ranking inherits that selection bias. More recent methods relax SCAR; see the survey by Bekker and Davis (2020). 19.3.3 Common strategies Two-step methods first identify reliable negatives in the unlabeled data and then train an ordinary classifier. Spy technique: hide a random subset of seed members (“spies”) in the unlabeled set, train seed versus unlabeled, and treat unlabeled records that score below most spies as reliable negatives (Liu et al., 2002). Initial-classifier approach: train seed versus unlabeled, then take the lowest-scoring unlabeled records as reliable negatives. Bagging PU trains many classifiers, each on the positives against a random subsample of unlabeled records, and averages their scores (Mordelet and Vert, 2014). Class-prior methods estimate \(c\) (or the positive share) and correct the classifier’s output, as in Elkan and Noto. 19.3.4 Worked example: a retailer’s lookalike audience The numbers are invented and kept round so the logic is easy to follow. Setup. A retailer’s addressable population has 1,000,000 people. Suppose (unknown to the analyst) 200,000 of them would become high-value customers. The seed audience is 60,000 known high-value customers. So the seed captures \(c = 60{,}000 / 200{,}000 = 0.30\) of all true positives. Step 1: the naive model. The analyst trains “seed versus everyone else.” The model outputs \(P(s = 1 \mid x)\): the probability that a person is in the seed, not the probability that they are high value. Person Naive score \(P(s=1 \mid x)\) Corrected \(P(y=1 \mid x) = \text{score} / 0.30\) Ana 0.15 0.50 Ben 0.06 0.20 Cem 0.01 0.03 What changes and what does not. Ranking is the same. Ana > Ben > Cem under both columns. If the media plan says “target the top 100,000 people,” the naive model already picks the right people (under SCAR). Probabilities and sizes change. The naive scores sum to roughly the seed size (about 60,000) across the population, so the naive model implies “about 60,000 people like our customers exist.” The corrected scores sum to about 200,000. If a client asks “how big is the opportunity?” or “how many conversions should we expect?”, the naive answer is too low by a factor of about three. Step 2: the spy technique in numbers. To find reliable negatives, hide 6,000 seed members (10%) as “spies” inside the unlabeled population and train seed versus unlabeled. Suppose 95% of spies score above 0.08. Unlabeled people scoring below 0.08 look less like customers than almost every real customer does, so they are treated as reliable negatives. A second model is then trained on seed versus those reliable negatives. Step 3: when the assumption fails. Suppose the seed came only from the email loyalty program. Mobile-app-only customers are high value but rarely in the program, so they are under-represented in the seed. The model learns “looks like an email subscriber” rather than “looks like a high-value customer.” It ranks valuable mobile-only prospects low, and no PU correction fixes that, because the correction assumes the seed is a random sample of all positives. The remedies are a better seed (combine sources), features that describe selection, or methods that relax SCAR. To see how class overlap distorts audience sizing while leaving the ranking unchanged, open tab 3 of the Classification Lab. 19.3.5 A runnable illustration The simulation below knows the true labels, so it can show both what the Elkan–Noto correction does and when it fails. Results were produced with scikit-learn 1.5; other versions may differ slightly. import numpy as np from sklearn.datasets import make_classification from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split def pu_demo(class_sep: float, label_freq: float = 0.3, seed: int = 42) -> None: rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=10, n_informative=5, weights=[0.8, 0.2], class_sep=class_sep, random_state=seed) # Seed audience: a random 30% of true positives (the SCAR assumption) s = ((y == 1) & (rng.random(len(y)) < label_freq)).astype(int) X_fit, X_rest, s_fit, s_rest, _, y_rest = train_test_split( X, s, y, test_size=0.4, random_state=seed, stratify=s) X_hold, X_te, s_hold, _, _, y_te = train_test_split( X_rest, s_rest, y_rest, test_size=0.5, random_state=seed, stratify=s_rest) # Naive model: seed (s=1) vs everyone else treated as negative clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_fit, s_fit) # Elkan-Noto: c = P(s=1 | y=1), estimated on held-out seed members c_hat = clf.predict_proba(X_hold[s_hold == 1])[:, 1].mean() p_pos = np.clip(clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1] / c_hat, 0, 1) print(f"class_sep={class_sep}: c_hat={c_hat:.2f} (true {label_freq}), " f"AUC={roc_auc_score(y_te, p_pos):.3f}, " f"est. positive share={p_pos.mean():.3f} (true {y_te.mean():.3f})") for sep in [1.0, 3.0]: pu_demo(sep) class_sep=1.0: c_hat=0.11 (true 0.3), AUC=0.832, est. positive share=0.465 (true 0.207) class_sep=3.0: c_hat=0.24 (true 0.3), AUC=0.981, est. positive share=0.209 (true 0.207) Interpretation. When positives and negatives are well separated (class_sep=3.0), the estimate of \(c\) is close to the truth and the estimated positive share is accurate. When the classes overlap (class_sep=1.0), which is typical of behavioral marketing data, the estimator of \(c\) is badly biased downward. The positive share is then overstated by more than a factor of two. This estimator assumes the classifier gives true positives a score near \(c\), which fails when classes overlap. The ranking (AUC) is identical to the naive classifier in both cases, illustrating consequence 1 above. Takeaway: use PU corrections for audience sizing only after checking their assumptions. For audience ranking, the larger risks are selection bias in the seed and leakage, not the missing negatives. 19.3.6 An enterprise example IBM has described using PU learning in its account-based marketing to find lookalike accounts. The model scores a user–item pair by their similarity: \[ \text{score}(u, v) = u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^{d} u_i v_i \quad \text{or} \quad \cos(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\lVert u \rVert \, \lVert v \rVert}. \] The dot product rewards both direction and magnitude. Cosine similarity uses only direction, which removes the effect of vector length, often a proxy for popularity. The idea goes back to the deep structured semantic model for search (Huang et al., 2013). YouTube’s candidate-generation network (Covington et al., 2016) and its sampling-bias-corrected two-tower model (Yi et al., 2019) made it standard for large-scale recommendation. 19.4.2 Why it scales: late interaction and approximate search The towers interact only at the final similarity step (“late fusion”). That separation enables a two-stage system: Offline: compute embeddings for every item (or every user) and store them in a vector index. Online: compute the query embedding and run an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search to retrieve the top candidates quickly, even across very large catalogs. Because the towers never see each other’s features before the final step, they cannot model detailed user–item feature crosses. Production systems therefore add a ranking stage. A heavier model, such as Wide & Deep (Cheng et al., 2016) or DeepFM (Guo et al., 2017), re-scores the few hundred retrieved candidates and applies business rules such as diversity, frequency caps, and brand safety. 19.4.3 Using embeddings for lookalike audiences Once user embeddings exist, lookalike modeling becomes a search problem: Centroid search: average the seed users’ embeddings and retrieve the nearest non-seed users. This is simple but assumes a single, compact seed cluster. Multi-anchor search: cluster the seed first, then search around each cluster center. This works better when the seed contains distinct personas. Classifier in embedding space: train a PU or ordinary classifier on the embeddings, combining the two approaches in this chapter. 19.4.4 Worked example: dot product versus cosine Real embeddings have dozens to hundreds of dimensions that have no names. For intuition, imagine three dimensions: sport, tech, and family. A user who mostly buys sports gear, sometimes family items, and rarely tech has the embedding \(u = (0.9, 0.1, 0.4)\). Three candidate items: Item Embedding \(v\) Length \(\lVert v \rVert\) Dot product \(u \cdot v\) Cosine Running shoes (0.8, 0.0, 0.3) 0.85 0.84 0.99 Phone case (very popular) (1.5, 1.2, 1.0) 2.17 1.87 0.87 Kids’ bike (0.2, 0.1, 0.9) 0.93 0.55 0.60 How to read it: The running shoes point in almost exactly the user’s direction (cosine 0.99): they are the best match in taste. The phone case has a long vector. In many trained models, popular items end up with larger embeddings because they appear in many interactions. The dot product rewards that length, so the phone case wins on dot product even though it matches the user’s taste less well. Neither metric is “right.” Dot product mixes relevance with popularity, which can raise click-through but narrows exposure. Cosine focuses on taste, which helps niche items and new products. Choose deliberately and evaluate both. 19.4.5 Worked example: why a single centroid can fail Suppose the seed has two personas in a two-dimensional embedding: bargain hunters near (1, 0) and premium buyers near (0, 1). Their centroid is (0.5, 0.5). Prospect Distance to centroid Distance to nearest persona Bargain-hunter-like (0.9, 0.1) 0.57 0.14 Premium-like (0.1, 0.9) 0.57 0.14 In-between (0.5, 0.5) 0.00 0.71 A centroid search ranks the in-between prospect first even though that person resembles neither real persona. Clustering the seed first and searching around each cluster center (multi-anchor search) ranks the two persona-like prospects first, which is what the client wants. 19.4.6 Training choices that matter Negative sampling. Interaction logs contain mostly positives (clicks, purchases). Negatives usually come from in-batch sampling or random sampling. In-batch sampling over-represents popular items, which Yi et al. correct for. The ratio of negatives to positives is a tuning choice, not a fixed rule. Popularity bias. Without correction, retrieval favors already-popular items and users who resemble the majority. Common responses are sampling corrections, re-weighting rare items, and diversity rules at the ranking stage. Cold start. Because the towers use content and context features, new users and items get embeddings from their metadata. Their quality still needs separate evaluation. Privacy. User embeddings derived from behavior are personal data in many jurisdictions. Govern them like the raw data. On Databricks, embeddings are typically stored in Delta tables and served through AI Search (formerly Vector Search) for ANN retrieval. Check the current documentation for supported index types and limits. 19.5 Typed decision models: Jev and “System One” classification 19.5.1 Why a different model type Generative LLMs can classify text, but for high-volume pipelines they bring three costs: latency and token cost, because they generate output token by token; format errors when asked to return JSON; and free-text output that downstream code must parse and validate. Teams already address these with structured-output features, small fine-tuned encoders (BERT-style classifiers), or embedding-plus-classifier pipelines. A newer option is a model built only for typed decisions. 19.5.2 What Jev is TypeSafe AI describes Jev as the first “System One model,” a name borrowed from Kahneman’s distinction between fast, intuitive thinking and slow, deliberate thinking (TypeSafe announcement, Sep 2026). Jev takes a piece of state (text or JSON) and one or more typed questions, and returns only structured answers. It never generates prose, explanations, or code. According to the TypeSafe documentation, it supports three question primitives: Primitive Question form Returns Marketing example Choice Pick one option from a list The chosen option, a probability for each option, confidence Route an inquiry to billing, support, or sales Score Place the state on an ordered rubric A score, probabilities over levels, confidence Rate lead urgency or customer frustration Noul Is this statement true? A single probability that the answer is yes “Does this email request a refund?” TypeSafe says it trains Jev with a method it calls Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), which it contrasts with the RLHF used for chat models. It has not published the method’s details. 19.5.3 Confidence is not calibration TypeSafe’s documentation defines confidence as a summary of how concentrated the probability distribution is (TypeSafe: Confidence): Choice, with \(n\) options and top probability \(p_{\max}\): \[\text{confidence} = \frac{p_{\max} - 1/n}{1 - 1/n},\] which is 0 for an even split and 1 for certainty. Noul, with probability \(p\): the suggested summary is \(\text{confidence} = |2p - 1|\). Score, with level probabilities \(p_i\) and most likely level \(m\): \[\text{confidence} = \max\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{\sum_i p_i \lvert i - m \rvert}{\text{MAD}_{\text{unif}}}\right),\] where \(\text{MAD}_{\text{unif}}\) is the same average distance for an even spread across all levels, measured from the middle level. Uncertainty between adjacent levels lowers confidence less than uncertainty between distant levels. 19.5.4 Worked examples: computing confidence by hand Choice: routing a customer email to one of four teams (\(n = 4\), so an even split gives each team \(1/n = 0.25\)). Returned probabilities (Billing, Support, Sales, Cancel) \(p_{\max}\) Confidence 0.70, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05 0.70 \((0.70 - 0.25)/(1 - 0.25) = 0.60\) 0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10 0.40 \((0.40 - 0.25)/(0.75) = 0.20\) 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25 0.25 0.00 Read confidence as “how far the top answer stands above a coin-toss among the options,” rescaled to run from 0 to 1. Score: rating complaint urgency on five levels numbered 0 (calm) to 4 (furious). For five levels, an even spread has an average distance of 1.2 levels from the middle level, so \(\text{MAD}_{\text{unif}} = 1.2\). Case Probabilities on levels 0–4 Most likely level Average distance \(\sum p_i \lvert i - m \rvert\) Confidence A: torn between angry and furious 0, 0, 0, 0.6, 0.4 3 \(0.4 \times 1 = 0.4\) \(1 - 0.4/1.2 = 0.67\) B: torn between angry and calm 0.4, 0, 0, 0.6, 0 3 \(0.4 \times 3 = 1.2\) \(1 - 1.2/1.2 = 0.00\) Both cases put 60% on level 3, yet A has useful confidence and B has none. In A the model only hesitates about how angry the customer is. In B it cannot tell whether the customer is angry or calm, which is useless for prioritizing. Noul: “Does this email request a refund?” Returned \(p\) Confidence \(\lvert 2p - 1 \rvert\) Reading 0.94 0.88 Confident yes 0.55 0.10 Close to a coin toss 0.06 0.88 Confident no Confidently wrong. In the first Choice row, suppose the email actually came from a customer about to cancel. The model said Billing with confidence 0.60, and it was wrong. Nothing in the formula can reveal that; only comparing predictions with true labels across many emails can. That comparison is calibration, described next. Try your own distributions in tab 1 of the Classification Lab. These formulas describe the shape of the distribution, not whether it is right. A model can be confidently wrong. Calibration means that among cases predicted at 90%, about 90% are actually positive. Calibration is an empirical property that you must measure on your own labeled data. TypeSafe says Jev is trained for calibrated probabilities, but no calibration evaluation (such as reliability diagrams or expected calibration error) was found in its published materials as of October 2026. 19.5.5 Vendor-reported performance TypeSafe reports [Vendor]: end-to-end latency of roughly 70 to 500 milliseconds, against seconds for frontier LLMs; input pricing of $0.042 per million tokens, with output not billed; and that answers always match the declared schema, so type errors are impossible by construction. TypeSafe notes that its published evaluations were run from its own machines and that its workflow benchmarks were built by its own team. Schema conformance by construction is credible. Accuracy, calibration, and real-world latency still need independent testing. As of October 2026 the model was proprietary and served through TypeSafe’s hosted API; access terms may change. 19.5.6 Where a typed decision model fits Routing and triage: a Choice question picks the destination while a Score question rates urgency, evaluated on the same input. Text-to-feature labeling: turn reviews, survey open-ends, or call notes into categorical features for downstream models. Guardrails for agents: ask a Noul question such as “Is this proposed action read-only?” before an agent runs a tool. This complements deterministic permissions and hooks; it does not replace them. Design questions atomically: ask one factor per question, and let ordinary code combine the answers into the final action. This keeps each probability interpretable and testable. 19.6 Validating classifiers before automation Whatever the model, decide thresholds from evidence, not from reported confidence. Build a labeled sample that represents production traffic, including rare and ambiguous cases. Have humans label it, and measure agreement between labelers. Run in shadow mode. Score live traffic in parallel with the current process without affecting decisions. Measure discrimination and calibration separately. Discrimination (AUC, precision at the chosen threshold) says whether the model ranks well. Calibration says whether its probabilities can be taken at face value. Set thresholds from costs. Choose automation thresholds from the cost of each error type, and route the uncertain middle band to people or to a slower model. Monitor drift. Re-check calibration when products, campaigns, or language change. A minimal calibration check: import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss def calibration_report(y_true, p_pred, n_bins: int = 10) -> pd.DataFrame: """Compare predicted probabilities with observed frequencies on labeled data.""" frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_true, p_pred, n_bins=n_bins, strategy="quantile") print(f"Brier score: {brier_score_loss(y_true, p_pred):.3f}") return pd.DataFrame({"mean_predicted": mean_pred.round(2), "observed_rate": frac_pos.round(2)}) # Simulated shadow-mode log: an overconfident classifier rng = np.random.default_rng(7) true_p = rng.uniform(0, 1, 2_000) y = rng.binomial(1, true_p) p_reported = np.clip(0.5 + 1.6 * (true_p - 0.5), 0.01, 0.99) # pushed toward 0/1 print(calibration_report(y, p_reported, n_bins=5)) Brier score: 0.180 mean_predicted observed_rate 0 0.01 0.10 1 0.18 0.30 2 0.49 0.51 3 0.82 0.68 4 0.99 0.91 The simulated model reports 0.99 when the observed rate is 0.91, and 0.01 when it is 0.10. A threshold of “automate above 0.95” would therefore be much less safe than it appears. If calibration is poor but ranking is good, recalibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. Do not tune the threshold on the same sample you use to report performance. 19.6.1 Worked example: from calibration to an automation threshold Checking calibration in plain terms. In shadow mode, a classifier flags 1,000 emails as “refund request” with probability around 0.90. Human reviewers check them and find that 760 really are refund requests. The observed rate is 0.76, not 0.90, so the model is overconfident in that range. Repeat the check for other probability bands (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, …) to draw the full calibration curve. Choosing a threshold from costs. Suppose the app escalates likely churn emails to a retention specialist: escalating an email that was not churn risk (false positive) wastes about $1 of specialist time; missing a real churn-risk email (false negative) loses about $9 in expected customer value. With calibrated probability \(p\), escalating costs \((1 - p) \times 1\) in expectation and not escalating costs \(p \times 9\). Escalation is worth it when \(p \times 9 > (1 - p) \times 1\), that is, when \[ p > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}} = \frac{1}{1 + 9} = 0.10. \] Two lessons follow: The threshold comes from the business costs, not from the model. Here escalating at only 10% probability is rational because misses are nine times as costly as false alarms. A default threshold of 0.5 would miss many saveable customers. The rule only works with calibrated probabilities. If the model’s “0.10” really means 0.03, the threshold is wrong. Calibrate first, then apply the cost rule. State the SCAR assumption, explain why ranking is unaffected by the missing negatives but sizing is not, and propose an experiment to validate lift. “Why use a two-tower model?” It separates user and item encoders so that embeddings can be precomputed and searched with approximate nearest neighbors. The trade-off is weaker feature interactions, which a ranking stage recovers. “Can I trust a model’s confidence score?” Only after measuring calibration on representative labeled data. Concentration of probability is not accuracy. “LLM or classifier for ticket routing?” For stable categories at high volume, use a classifier or typed decision model with measured calibration. Reserve generative models for ambiguous cases and explanations. 19.10 Key takeaways Lookalike modeling is a positive-unlabeled problem. The SCAR assumption determines what corrections are valid, and seed selection bias is often the bigger risk. Two-tower networks make embedding-based retrieval and lookalikes scale; negative sampling and popularity bias need deliberate design. Typed decision models such as Jev return structured probabilities instead of text. Their schema guarantees are credible by design, but accuracy and calibration claims require your own validation. Confidence measures how concentrated a distribution is; calibration measures whether probabilities match reality. Automate only on measured calibration. Validate in shadow mode first, then prove business value with experiments. 19.11 References Positive-unlabeled learning Elkan, C., and Noto, K. (2008).
