Chapter 20 Supervisor Agents and Multi-Agent Systems on Databricks 20.1 Introduction A single agent with a few tools can answer many questions. Real analytics questions often cross domains, though: “Why did conversions drop for the spring campaign, and which audience should we test next?” needs campaign metrics, audience overlap, research reports, and perhaps a modeling job. A supervisor agent handles this by coordinating specialized agents and tools. It decides who should answer each part, delegates, and combines the results. This chapter covers: the supervisor pattern and when multiple agents help or hurt; Databricks Supervisor Agent: how it works and how to build one; what Databricks recommends for new work as of October 2026; and a marketing-analytics example with descriptions, test questions, and evaluation. It builds on MCP (Chapter 16), context and harness engineering (Chapter 17), and the analytics tools in Chapter 19. Status check (October 2026). On 6 October 2026 the Databricks documentation labeled Supervisor Agent a legacy offering. For new low-code agents it recommends Genie Agents. To coordinate multiple agents in code it recommends the Agent Bricks CLI, which was in Beta at the time of writing. The related Supervisor API (Beta) was deprecated, with end of life on 30 September 2026. The supervisor pattern in this chapter remains current; the specific product is likely to change. Check the Supervisor Agent page and What is Agent Bricks? before building. 20.2 The supervisor pattern 20.2.1 What a supervisor does A supervisor is an agent whose tools are other agents (and ordinary tools). For each request it: interprets the question and breaks it into parts; routes each part to the subagent or tool whose description fits best; delegates and collects the answers; and synthesizes one response, or asks the user to clarify. Anthropic describes the same idea as the orchestrator–workers workflow: a central model breaks down a task, delegates subtasks to workers, and synthesizes their results (Building effective agents). 20.2.2 Common multi-agent shapes Pattern How it works Good for Router Sends the whole request to one specialist Clearly separable domains (billing vs. analytics) Supervisor Splits the request, calls several specialists, combines results Cross-domain questions Hierarchical A supervisor calls other supervisors Large organizations with domain teams Pipeline Fixed sequence of steps Repeatable workflows; often better as ordinary code 20.2.3 When multiple agents help, and when they hurt They help when: domains have different data, permissions, and owners (each team curates its own Genie Agent); a specialist needs a focused context, which is the isolate technique from Chapter 17; and subtasks can run independently and be combined. They hurt when: the task needs one shared, detailed understanding that gets lost in handoffs; latency and cost matter, because every delegation adds model calls; and a fixed workflow would do. A scheduled job is simpler, cheaper, and easier to test than an agent deciding the steps each time. A good rule: start with one well-scoped agent, and add a supervisor only when routing between distinct, well-defined specialists is the actual problem. 20.3 Databricks Supervisor Agent The facts in this section come from the Supervisor Agent documentation as of 6 October 2026. 20.3.1 What it provides Supervisor Agent builds a supervisor system that coordinates Genie Agents, agent endpoints, Unity Catalog functions, MCP servers, and custom agents. It produces a serving endpoint that you can query from AI Playground, the API, or a Databricks App. Domain experts can improve its routing with natural-language feedback. Databricks lists use cases such as market analysis across research reports and usage data, internal-process questions, and customer-service answers. 20.3.2 Requirements Serverless compute and Unity Catalog enabled, in a supported region. Access to Model Serving and to a serverless usage policy with a nonzero budget. At least one subagent ready to use. End users need explicit access to each subagent (next table). 20.3.3 Supported subagents and required end-user permissions Subagent or tool Required end-user permission Genie Agent Access to the Genie Agent and its underlying Unity Catalog objects Published dashboard CAN VIEW on the dashboard Knowledge Assistant endpoint CAN QUERY on the endpoint Model serving endpoint CAN QUERY on the endpoint Unity Catalog function EXECUTE on the function Unity Catalog table SELECT, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA Unity Catalog volume READ VOLUME, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA AI Search index (Delta Sync only) SELECT, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA Another Supervisor Agent CAN QUERY on it Unity Catalog MCP Service EXECUTE, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA Custom MCP server or custom agent on Databricks Apps CAN_USE on the app Web search (built in) No extra permission; the user approves each search A supervisor can use up to 50 agents and tools. Access control is per user. End users reach only the subagents and data they are allowed to use. If a user can access none of the subagents, the supervisor ends the conversation. If they can access only some, it steers away from the others. This is the behavior an agency needs when different teams may see different clients’ data. 20.3.4 Built-in code execution Every supervisor includes a code execution tool. It runs model-generated Python (default), SQL, or shell commands in a sandboxed serverless session with no internet access. Its only data access is read-only access to the Unity Catalog tables and volumes added as tools, subject to the end user’s permissions. Databricks warns that running arbitrary code can expose data the agent can reach, so permissions and guardrails remain the customer’s responsibility. 20.3.5 Web search Web search uses the databricks-gpt-5 Foundation Model API regardless of the model that powers the supervisor. The workspace must allow that model, and web search is unavailable in some regions and in workspaces with the Enhanced Security and Compliance add-on. The supervisor asks the user to approve each search before sending the query to the public web. Never let client data appear in a web query. 20.3.6 Building one: five steps Configure. Go to Agents → Create Agent → Supervisor Agent. Add tools and subagents, and write a description for each one; the supervisor routes based on these descriptions. Optionally add supervisor-level Instructions and a user-facing Description. Test. Chat in the right pane, or open the endpoint in AI Playground, where AI Judge and synthetic task generation may be available. Check that each question reaches the right subagent. Improve. In the Examples tab, add representative questions. Share the configuration page with subject-matter experts (they need Can Manage on the agent and access to the subagents). Experts attach natural-language Guidelines to questions, and guidelines take effect when saved. Manage permissions. Grant Can Manage (edit and improve) or Can Query (use the endpoint only) to users, groups, or service principals. Query the endpoint. From AI Playground, Get code provides curl and Python examples for applications such as a Streamlit app on Databricks Apps. 20.3.7 Managing supervisors with the SDK (Beta) The Databricks SDK for Python can create supervisors and manage their tools. From the documentation: from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient from databricks.sdk.service.supervisoragents import SupervisorAgent w = WorkspaceClient() supervisor_agent = SupervisorAgent( display_name="<display-name>", description="<description>", instructions="<instructions>", ) created = w.supervisor_agents.create_supervisor_agent(supervisor_agent=supervisor_agent) print(created) Tools (subagents) are added with w.supervisor_agents.create_tool(...), and their descriptions can be updated with update_tool. This lets a team keep supervisor configurations in version control and recreate them across workspaces. See the documentation for the tool types and fields. 20.3.8 Limitations At most 50 agents and tools per supervisor. AI Search subagents support only Delta Sync indexes. Web search has the regional and compliance restrictions above. It is a legacy offering, so plan for migration. 20.4 What to use for new work (October 2026) Need Databricks recommendation Notes Low-code agent over tables and documents Genie Agents Curated with Unity Catalog metadata, example SQL, instructions, and trusted assets Business users exploring data, dashboards, apps Genie One Can also be called as a tool by custom agents Custom agent in code, including multi-agent coordination Agent Bricks CLI (Beta) deploying to Agent Runtime Scaffolds a project, runs locally, deploys with managed memory, sessions, tools, and MLflow tracing Composing several agents, such as coding agents Omnigent Described by Databricks as a meta-harness Existing Supervisor Agent Keep running, plan migration Legacy; no new investment Sources: What is Agent Bricks?, September 2026 release notes. In code, the pattern stays the same. Databricks’ multi-agent app template builds an orchestrator that treats each subagent as a tool: Genie Agents reached through their MCP server, other agents on Databricks Apps, and serving endpoints. Each subagent has a name, an endpoint, and a detailed description to improve routing (multi-agent apps). That page uses the legacy agent server; follow the Agent Bricks CLI documentation for new deployments. What carries over regardless of product: clear subagent descriptions, per-user permissions, a labeled set of test questions, and expert guidelines. Building these now is not wasted if the product changes. 20.5 Worked example: a campaign insights supervisor An agency team wants one assistant for account leads that answers cross-domain questions about a client’s campaigns. 20.5.1 The specialists Subagent or tool Type What it covers campaign_performance Genie Agent over campaign metric views Spend, impressions, reach, conversions, CPA by channel, market, and week audience_overlap Unity Catalog function Size and overlap of two audience segments basket_affinity Unity Catalog function Precomputed support, confidence, and lift for product pairs lookalike_jobs Custom MCP server on Databricks Apps Start the validated lookalike job; check status and results research_library Document Q&A (Knowledge Assistant or AI Search index) Client briefs, research reports, past campaign learnings 20.5.2 Write descriptions that route well The supervisor routes on descriptions, so treat them as prompts. Compare: Weak: “Campaign data.” Strong: “Answers quantitative questions about this client’s paid-media campaigns: spend, impressions, reach, clicks, conversions, CPA, and ROAS by channel, market, campaign, and week, from 2024 onward. Use for ‘how much’, ‘how did it change’, and ‘which channel’ questions. Does not contain audience membership, product purchases, or research documents.” A strong description says what the tool covers, when to use it, and what it does not cover. The “does not” part prevents many routing errors. 20.5.3 Test questions and expected routing Question Expected route “What was CPA by channel last month in Germany?” campaign_performance “How much do our sports-fans and new-parents segments overlap?” audience_overlap “Which products are most often bought with running shoes?” basket_affinity “Why did spring conversions drop, and what did last year’s brief say about seasonality?” campaign_performance + research_library “Build a 3% lookalike from the loyalty seed.” lookalike_jobs, after confirmation “What’s the weather in Paris?” Politely decline (out of scope) “Show me individual customer emails in the seed.” Decline (personal data) 20.5.4 Expert guidelines Account leads and analysts add guidelines to example questions, such as: “When reporting CPA, always state the date range and currency.” “Do not compare markets with different currencies without converting.” “For lookalike requests, confirm the seed, size, and client before starting a job.” “Overlap results come from the function; never estimate overlap from memory.” “If a question mixes two clients, ask which client is meant.” 20.5.5 Agency-specific design choices Client separation. Use one supervisor per client, or Unity Catalog row filters and per-user permissions, so that no conversation can mix clients’ data. Test this explicitly with users who lack access. Numbers from tools. Display numeric results from tool outputs, not from the model’s prose. Apply the number-check sensor from Chapter 17. Actions need confirmation. Starting a job costs money; require explicit user confirmation and log who approved it. Web search off or tightly scoped. Client names or results must not appear in public web queries. 20.6 Evaluating a supervisor Evaluate two things separately: Routing accuracy. For each labeled question, did the supervisor call the expected subagents, and avoid the wrong ones? Trace data in MLflow shows which tools were called. Answer quality. Are the numbers correct (they should match the tool output exactly), is the answer grounded, and did the supervisor clarify or decline when it should? Practical steps: Build 30 to 50 labeled questions covering every subagent, multi-domain questions, out-of-scope requests, and permission edge cases. Run each question several times and report pass^k (all runs correct), not just one lucky run. Re-run the set after every change to descriptions, guidelines, or subagents. A better description for one tool can steal traffic from another. Use MLflow GenAI evaluation with code-based checks for routing and number matching, and LLM judges or expert review for answer quality. 20.7 Common pitfalls Pitfall Symptom Fix Overlapping descriptions Questions bounce between two subagents Make scopes exclusive; add “does not cover” lines Too many subagents Slow, inconsistent routing Merge narrow tools; add a supervisor only where domains truly differ Missing user permissions “I can’t help with that” for some users Grant access to each subagent, or explain the restriction Synthesized numbers The answer contains figures not in any tool output Render numbers from tool outputs; add a number check Silent actions Jobs started without approval Require confirmation for writing or spending actions Untested changes Quality drops after an edit Re-run the labeled question set after every change 20.8 Exercise: design a supervisor on paper List three to five specialists you already have or could build (a Genie Agent, two Unity Catalog functions, a document index). Write a strong description for each, including what it does not cover. Write 15 test questions with expected routes, including two multi-domain questions, two out-of-scope requests, and one permission edge case. Write five expert guidelines. Decide whether you need a supervisor at all, or whether one Genie Agent or a scheduled job would do. 20.9 Key takeaways A supervisor routes, delegates, and synthesizes across specialists; it is the orchestrator–workers pattern. Use multiple agents only when distinct domains, permissions, or contexts justify them; otherwise one agent or a fixed workflow is simpler. Databricks Supervisor Agent coordinates up to 50 agents and tools, enforces per-user access, includes sandboxed code execution, and improves through expert guidelines. As of October 2026, Supervisor Agent is legacy. Use Genie Agents for low-code work and the Agent Bricks CLI for custom multi-agent code. Descriptions, permissions, labeled test questions, and guidelines are durable assets that survive product changes. Evaluate routing and answer quality separately, repeatedly, and after every change. 20.10 References Databricks: Use Supervisor Agent to create a coordinated multi-agent system Databricks: What is Agent Bricks? A Course Labs: Walkthroughs A.1 Common setup A.2 Lab 1: Summarization with prompting and generation settings A.3 Lab 2: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA A.4 Lab 3: Detoxifying with RLHF (PPO) A.5 What the three labs show together

A Course Labs: Walkthroughs The course Generative AI with Large Language Models (DeepLearning.AI / AWS, Coursera) had three hands-on labs. All three used one task: summarizing dialogues with Flan-T5. Each lab applied one stage of the lifecycle (Section 1.7) to that task: prompting, then fine-tuning, then alignment. This appendix records what each lab did and what it teaches. It is written in my own words, and the course notebooks are not reproduced. About the numbers. Results below are as reported in the course labs, not reproduced here. They came from small samples and short training runs on 2023-era library versions. Read them as directional evidence. The libraries used (Hugging Face transformers, peft, trl, and evaluate) have changed their APIs since then, so check current documentation before rebuilding any of these workflows. A.1 Common setup Item Choice Model google/flan-t5-base: an instruction-tuned encoder–decoder model of about 250M parameters (Chapter 3) Data DialogSum (Chen et al. 2021): about 13,000 everyday and service dialogues, each with a human-written summary. Not part of Flan-T5’s training mixture. Task Generate a one- or two-sentence summary of a dialogue Reference The human summary, used for side-by-side reading and as the ROUGE reference Limits Flan-T5’s 512-token input limit; long dialogues get truncated A.2 Lab 1: Summarization with prompting and generation settings Goal. Find out how far prompting alone can take a small model, before any training. This is the first step with any new model and dataset. Steps: No instruction. Pass the raw dialogue to the model. The output was a continuation or fragment, not a summary. The model could not tell what task was wanted. Zero-shot instruction. Wrap the dialogue as “Summarize the following conversation. … Summary:”. The output became summary-like but missed nuance. Model-native template. Use one of the phrasings from Flan-T5’s own training templates (“Dialogue: … What was going on?”). This gave a modest improvement. Prompts that match the model’s instruction-tuning format tend to work better. One-shot and few-shot. Prepend one, then three, complete examples (dialogue plus human summary) before the target dialogue. One-shot helped; few-shot did not clearly beat one-shot on the example shown. Some few-shot prompts also exceeded the 512-token limit. Generation settings. Vary max_new_tokens, sampling on or off, and temperature (Section 1.6). Low temperature gave conservative, repeatable summaries. High temperature gave varied and sometimes incoherent ones. Lessons: With a small model, the instruction wording and format matter, and in-context examples give a limited lift. The course team’s rule of thumb was that more than five or six examples rarely help. Examples consume the context window. For a 512-token model this is a hard constraint. When prompting plateaus below the quality you need, fine-tune (Lab 2). A.3 Lab 2: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA Goal. Improve zero-shot summarization by fine-tuning on DialogSum, and compare full fine-tuning with parameter-efficient LoRA (Section 3.5). Steps: Format the data as instructions. Map each record to the prompt “Summarize the following conversation. {dialogue} Summary:”, with the human summary as the target. Tokenize, and split into training, validation, and test sets. Full instruction fine-tuning. Train all ~250M parameters with the Hugging Face Trainer. The in-lab run used a small subsample and very few steps to save time. A checkpoint trained longer offline was then loaded for evaluation. That checkpoint was about 945 MB, a full copy of the model. LoRA fine-tuning. Wrap the same base model with a LoRA configuration of rank \(r = 32\), a relatively high rank. That left about 1.4% of parameters trainable. Train the same way, then load an offline-trained adapter of about 14 MB. Inference. Load the adapter on top of the frozen base model with training disabled. That reported 0% trainable parameters and avoids allocating training state. Evaluate. Compare human, base-model, fully fine-tuned, and LoRA-tuned summaries, first by reading them and then with ROUGE (Section 3.6) on a larger held-out set. Reported results: Full fine-tuning clearly beat the base model on every ROUGE variant. The walkthrough quoted about 18 (ROUGE-1), 10 (ROUGE-2), 13 (ROUGE-L), and 13.7 (ROUGE-Lsum) “percent” higher. It did not say whether these are relative changes or absolute ROUGE points. The lecture summarized the same comparison as absolute ROUGE-1 gains of +0.19 (full) and +0.17 (LoRA), which suggests absolute points. LoRA scored about 1–2 points below full fine-tuning across the ROUGE metrics. It trained about 1.4% of the parameters and stored about 14 MB instead of about 945 MB. Lessons: A small amount of task-specific instruction data can lift a general instruct model substantially on a narrow task. LoRA gives up a little quality for large savings in training memory and storage. The base model can be shared, with one small adapter per task. Read outputs as well as metrics. A ROUGE gain says nothing directly about invented details or missing actions. A.4 Lab 3: Detoxifying with RLHF (PPO) Goal. Make the Lab 2 summarizer less likely to produce hateful or toxic language, using reinforcement learning against a reward model (Chapter 4). Components: Role What was used Policy The LoRA-tuned Flan-T5 from Lab 2, plus a value head. The head is a single linear layer from the 768-dimensional hidden state to a scalar: 768 weights plus 1 bias. Only the LoRA adapter and the value head were trained. Reference policy A frozen copy of the Lab 2 model, used for the KL penalty Reward model An off-the-shelf RoBERTa hate-speech classifier with two classes, not hate and hate. The logit of the “not hate” class was the reward. Algorithm PPO from the trl library, with batch size 16 and few PPO epochs to keep the run short Evaluation Mean and standard deviation of the classifier’s hate probability over generated summaries, before and after training Steps: Build prompts from DialogSum dialogues, sampling input lengths to fit the model’s context. Measure the baseline toxicity of the Lab 2 model’s summaries. For each batch: generate summaries, score each (prompt, summary) pair with the classifier, and pass the prompts, responses, and rewards to a PPO step. The KL divergence to the reference model was monitored so that the policy could not drift into reward hacking. Re-measure toxicity, and compare summaries and rewards before and after. Reported results. After a short run, rewards rose on many examples and mean toxicity fell “by a decent amount”. The KL divergence stayed roughly stable during training. The course noted that the effect was modest because DialogSum is not a toxic dataset to begin with. Training longer, on more toxic prompts, would show a larger difference. Lessons: Check the reward’s class index. The classifier put “not hate” at index Optimizing the wrong index would actively increase toxicity. Reward definitions deserve tests of their own. A classifier is a narrow reward. The policy is optimized towards whatever this one model measures, which is why the KL penalty and human review of samples matter (Section 4.4). PEFT makes RLHF affordable. Training only the adapter and the value head kept memory low. The reference policy could share the frozen base weights. A.5 What the three labs show together Lab Lifecycle stage Lever What changes Main cost 1 Adapt (prompting) Instructions, examples, generation settings Only the input Context tokens; limited ceiling 2 Adapt (fine-tuning) Supervised training, full or LoRA Weights or adapter Labelled data and compute 3 Align PPO against a reward model, with a KL penalty Adapter and value head Reward design, run stability, evaluation The progression is the one recommended throughout this part of the book: start with prompting, fine-tune when prompting plateaus, align when outputs must follow preferences that labels alone do not capture, and evaluate at every step.
